notes.title: The three parts of every ad: call out + value + CTA

How do I structure a short video ad from start to finish?
My ad gets views but no sign-ups, which part is broken?
What is the difference between writing a long ad and a short ad?
notes.summary: Every ad has three jobs in order: get noticed (call out), make them interested (value), and tell them what to do next (CTA).

notes.title: Ad testing budget: 2x 30-day cash per customer

When should I kill a Facebook ad that isn't getting results?

aliases: when to turn off an ad
notes.summary: Let a new ad spend up to twice the cash (profit) a new customer brings in within 30 days before killing it, or 1x if it produces no leads at all.

notes.title: Integrating with affiliates: three ways, easiest to hardest

Should my partners give away my service, sell a starter version, or sell my main product?
Can a gym or spa next door bundle my service into their packages?

notes.title: Affiliate payouts: max allowable CAC and three tiers

What should I pay partners for: sales, leads, or booked appointments?
How do I calculate the most I can afford to pay for a referred customer?
Should I pay affiliate commissions forever or cap them?
notes.summary: Decide exactly what behavior you're paying for, cap payouts at your maximum allowable CAC, and tier payouts so only proven affiliates get the full amount.

notes.title: Measuring affiliate returns: cost per affiliate vs profit they bring

How much is one partner or affiliate worth to my business over a year?
My affiliate program barely breaks even, what can I fix?
How do I compare the cost of recruiting a partner with the profit they bring?
notes.summary: For affiliates, compare the cost to acquire an affiliate with the gross profit (after payouts) from all the customers that affiliate sends.

notes.title: Affiliates: independent businesses that sell your stuff to their audience

Why would I sell to partners instead of selling directly to customers?
How can partners help my revenue keep growing every month instead of plateauing?
Is an affiliate program a good fit for my business?

notes.title: The agency dependency cycle (how agencies want you to use them)

notes.title: Use agencies to learn, then replace them with your team

When should I stop paying an agency and bring marketing in-house?

My cold list responses are dropping, where can I find fresher contacts?

notes.title: Personalise cold outreach so it feels like a warm reach-out
questions: How do I write a cold email that doesn't sound like spam?
What should I say in the first few seconds of a cold call so they don't hang up?
How much research should I do on a prospect before messaging them?
Does simpler wording really get more replies to cold emails?
notes.summary: Strangers don't know you, so make the message look like it came from someone who does: open with one to three things a friend would know about them.

notes.title: Test the constraint: fix the biggest drop-off first

Where are most of my leads dropping off, and how do I fix it?
Should I test my ad, my landing page, or my booking step first?
notes.summary: Every step before purchase is a drop-off point; put your testing where the most leads drop off, because the smallest improvement there creates the biggest gain.

notes.title: Content benchmarks: measure audience size and growth rate monthly

How often should I post and ask for the sale on social media?
Can I promote my offer in my very first post?
notes.summary: Track how big the audience is and how fast it grows each month, holding your posting and ask cadence constant so the feedback means something.

Why don't people share my content or come back for more?

How do I plan or script a piece of content so it works?

My ads have stopped finding new winners, how do I keep innovating?
Is it okay to spend on marketing tests that might not pay back?

notes.title: Calculating returns from lead-getting employees

Should I fire my salespeople or fix my marketing when sales are low?

notes.title: Why a business that runs without you makes you wealthy

notes.title: Make your first five customers free
questions: Should I give my new service away free to my first clients?
I have no track record yet, how do I get my first testimonials?
Isn't working for free undervaluing myself when I'm just starting?
What should I ask free beta customers to do in return?
notes.summary: When launching a new product or service, give it to the first five people free in exchange for using it, giving feedback and leaving a review; the goal is learning, not earning.

notes.title: Follow up more times, more ways, then recycle the list after 3-6 months
questions: How many times should I follow up with a lead who doesn't respond?
Should I follow up by phone, text, or email?
When can I re-contact an old prospect list that didn't reply?
Is it okay to call after sending an email nobody answered?
notes.summary: Contact each lead several times across several channels as if you really needed to reach them, then restart the list a few months later.

notes.title: Turn best free content and UGC into paid ads
questions: Which content should I turn into ads?
Can customer reviews and videos be used as ads?
How do I lower the cost of making ad creative?
notes.summary: Your best-performing free content usually makes your best paid ads, and customer user-generated content is a free, steady supply of ad creative.

notes.title: Give away the secrets, sell the implementation
questions: Am I giving away too much for free in my content or consultations?
Will people still pay me if I teach everything for free?
How good should my free content be compared to my paid product?
notes.summary: Make free stuff as good as your paid stuff: give so much value up front that people feel obligated to pay you for implementation.

notes.title: Give-to-ask ratio and 'give until they ask'
questions: How often can I promote my offer on social media without losing followers?
How many value posts should I share for every sales post?
Should I keep giving free content until people ask to buy?
notes.summary: Deposit goodwill with rewarding content before withdrawing it with asks; to grow, over-give, and ideally keep giving publicly until people ask privately to buy.

notes.title: Goodwill: value minus price drives word of mouth
questions: Customers say they love us, so why does almost nobody recommend us to friends?
Should I drop my prices to get more people talking about my business?
Why are my clients embarrassed or reluctant to tell others about my product?
How do I make my service remarkable enough that people bring their friends?
notes.summary: Businesses lack referrals because their product isn't as good as they think and because they don't ask; the fix is building goodwill — the gap between value delivered and price paid — by adding value, not cutting price.

notes.title: Seven headline components from news (use at least two)
questions: What makes people actually click on a title or email subject line?
How do I write hooks for my videos that grab attention?
My ad headlines get ignored, what ingredients should a good headline have?
Why do news stories get attention and how can I copy that in marketing?
notes.summary: Headlines tell the audience why to consume; news research points to seven components that drive interest, and a good headline uses at least two.

notes.title: Hidden costs: when you can't even give it away free
questions: Why won't people take my offer even when I give it away for free?
Nobody signs up for my free trial, what am I doing wrong?
What should I ask a prospect who says no so I can fix my offer?
Should I keep cutting my price if nobody is buying?
notes.summary: If people turn down your free offer, your "free" thing is still too expensive because of hidden costs: the time, effort and sacrifice needed to get results.

notes.title: Hormozi's high-ROI habit stack for open-to-goal work
questions: How should a business owner structure their workday to get more done?
I get pulled into meetings and fires all day, how do I protect focus time?
Is waking up early actually worth it for running a business?
When during the day should I do my marketing work?
notes.summary: Wake early, start work immediately, and protect the first ~8 hours from meetings so your most productive hours go to your most important work — usually advertising.

notes.title: Hinge method: get a three-way introduction for every referral
questions: A client mentioned a friend who needs my service, how do I actually connect with them?
How do I stop referrals from going cold after a customer gives me a name?
What is the best way to get a customer to introduce me to someone by text?
notes.summary: When a customer offers a referral, make the introduction happen right then as a three-way connection instead of just collecting a name.

notes.title: Hire experience, not potential, to run lead-getting departments
questions: Should I hire someone experienced or promote from within to run my sales outreach team?
My cold calling department keeps failing, is it the people leading it?
What kind of person should I hire to head up marketing or paid media?
When is it worth paying more for a senior hire instead of training someone?
notes.summary: For people-heavy, operationally complex lead channels, put an experienced leader in charge — ideally one who knows more than you.

notes.title: Infinite ads: 30 call-outs x 10 bodies
questions: How can I test lots of video ads without spending a fortune on production?
How many ad variations should I make each week?
My video ads stop working quickly, how do I produce fresh creative cheaply?
Which part of a video ad is most worth testing?
notes.summary: Record about 10 new main ads a week plus 30+ different opening lines, then combine them to test hundreds of variations cheaply.

notes.title: How to ask in content: integrated vs intermittent asks
questions: How often should I promote my product in my podcast or videos without losing followers?
How do I sell to my audience without annoying them?
Should my social posts push my free download or my paid program?
Where should I put the call to action in a newsletter or blog post?
Is it okay to ask people to like, subscribe and buy all in one video?
notes.summary: If you must monetise content, treat asks as commercials inside your own program, either woven into each piece (integrated) or as occasional ask-only pieces (intermittent).

notes.title: The internal Core Four: get employees the way you get customers
questions: I can't find good employees, how do I attract more job applicants?
How do I recruit staff the same way I find customers?
Where should a small business look for new hires besides job boards?
Should I use staffing agencies or employee referrals to fill roles?
notes.summary: Recruiting is just advertising to potential employees, so every customer-getting method has a hiring equivalent.

notes.title: Landing pages: three simple layouts and message match
questions: What should my landing page look like to collect emails from ads?
People click my ad but don't fill out the form, what's wrong?
Do I need a fancy website to capture leads from Facebook ads?
What should I put on the page people land on after clicking an ad?
notes.summary: Capture contact info with a dead-simple landing page that matches the ad and frames the opt-in as consistent with the click they just made.

notes.title: Lead: a person you can contact
questions: What actually counts as a lead in my business?
My team counts leads differently, how should we define them for reporting?
Is a bought email list or a website click really a lead?
notes.summary: A lead is simply a person you can contact, nothing more.

notes.title: Choosing among lead getters, and sticking with one
questions: How long should I try a new marketing channel before giving up on it?
Should I build referrals, hire staff, use an agency or find partners first?
My first months of ads lost money, should I switch to something else?
In what order do businesses usually add new sources of customers?
notes.summary: Each lead getter has a distinct strength and they tend to arrive in a natural order; whichever you pick, expect three to six months to crack a new lead source and don't switch after early losses.

notes.title: Lead getters: getting other people to advertise for you
questions: I'm maxed out doing all the marketing myself, how do I get others to bring in customers?
How do I scale lead generation beyond my own hours?
Who else besides me can bring new customers into my business?
How do the biggest companies get leads without the founder doing the work?
aliases: getting others to sell for you
notes.summary: Only two kinds of people can tell strangers about your stuff — you and everyone else — so the highest-leverage lead machine gets other people ("lead getters") doing the Core Four for you, and ideally recruiting more lead getters.

notes.title: Lead-getting employees: trading doing for managing
questions: When should I hire someone to do my marketing and outreach for me?
I'm the bottleneck on getting new clients, how do I hand it off?
Should I hire experienced marketers or train beginners to generate leads?
How much of my time can I free up by managing instead of doing outreach?
notes.summary: Employees you train to run ads, post content and do outreach get you leads the same way you did — more of them means more leads and less of your own work.

notes.title: Example: a $25 lead magnet that cuts customer acquisition cost 3x
questions: Is it worth spending money on a free giveaway to get more sales calls?
How can a freebie lower my cost to get a customer even though it costs me to deliver?
My client refuses to pay for a free offer, how do I show them the numbers?
notes.summary: Worked numbers showing why a lead magnet that costs money to deliver still lowers acquisition cost.

notes.title: Four lead magnet delivery mechanisms (12 combinations with the three types)
questions: What formats can a free giveaway take besides an ebook?
Should my free offer be a tool, a course, a free service or a physical sample?
My free download stopped converting, how do I make fresh versions of it?
How can a local service business offer something free to attract leads?
notes.summary: Deliver a lead magnet as software, information, a service or a physical product; crossed with the three types that gives up to 12 lead magnets for one narrow problem.

notes.title: Make the lead magnet easy to consume in every format
questions: People download my free guide but never read it, how do I fix that?
Should I offer my free content as video, audio and text?
How do I get more people to actually use the freebie they signed up for?
notes.summary: Making a lead magnet easier to consume can raise take rates and consumption by 2-4x or more for the same work.

notes.title: Test the lead magnet's name: headline, then image, then subheadline
questions: How do I know which title for my free guide will get the most signups?
What should I test first on a giveaway, the title, image or description?
How can I test a product or course name cheaply before launching?
Nobody is interested in my free offer, could the name be the problem?
notes.summary: How a lead magnet is presented matters more than anything else, so test its headline, image and subheadline, in that order.

notes.title: Seven steps to create an effective lead magnet
questions: How do I create a free offer that actually brings in good leads?
What is the process for building a freebie that leads to paid sales?
I'm struggling to get leads, what free thing should I make first?
How do I check whether my existing freebie is any good?
notes.summary: Hormozi's seven-step process for building a lead magnet so good people feel stupid saying no, even though it's free.

notes.title: Three types of lead magnets: reveal the problem, sample/trial, one step of many
questions: What kind of free offer works best for a recurring service like pest control or hosting?
Should I give away a free assessment, a free sample, or part of my service?
How can a free audit or inspection lead to paid work?
What free thing can I offer if my service solves a complicated problem?
notes.summary: Lead magnets solve a problem in one of three ways: they diagnose a problem, give a brief sample of the core offer, or give away one step of a multi-step solution.

notes.title: Lead magnet: a complete solution to a narrow problem that reveals the next one
questions: What should I give away for free to attract people who will later buy?
My expensive service gets no inquiries, how do I get people interested first?
Why do businesses give away freebies and how do they make money from it?
What makes a free offer good enough that people want more?
notes.summary: A lead magnet is a low-cost or free offer that fully solves one narrow problem and, once solved, reveals another problem your core offer solves.

notes.title: Lower promises until close rate dips, then over-deliver
questions: Customers are satisfied but not raving about us, what should I change?
Am I overpromising in my sales pitch and hurting referrals?
How much should I promise clients so they end up delighted?
Our delivery team can't keep up with what sales promised, how do I fix that?
notes.summary: Since you set customer expectations, set them slightly lower than what you deliver so the product feels remarkable — but stop lowering before it hurts sales.

notes.title: LTGP:CAC ratio and the 3:1 threshold
questions: How much can I afford to spend to get one customer?
Is my problem my ads or my pricing and business model?
What ratio of customer value to acquisition cost do I need to scale?
Should I measure customer lifetime value using revenue or profit?
My ads are profitable but growth is stuck, what number should I check?
notes.summary: Measure advertising efficiency as lifetime gross profit per customer divided by cost to acquire a customer; below 3:1 businesses struggle to scale, above it they take off.

notes.title: Make all content for strangers
questions: My followers love my posts but my audience isn't growing, why?
Should I use inside jokes and references for my loyal fans?
How do I make social media content that new people will share?
notes.summary: Create every piece as if the viewer has never heard of you; strangers then like and share it and the audience grows faster.

notes.title: The many-sided die: you can't lose if you don't quit
questions: My first few ads all failed, should I give up on marketing?
Why do competitors seem luckier at getting customers than me?
How do I stay motivated when nothing in my marketing works yet?
notes.summary: A parable for learning to advertise: everyone rolls a die with an unknown number of sides and one green side; every green turns another side green, so whoever keeps rolling eventually rolls green most of the time.

notes.title: Monthly product improvement loop
questions: How do I keep improving my product or service in a systematic way?
What should I do with customer complaints and support tickets?
How do I fix the most common reason customers struggle with my program?
How do I test a product change before rolling it out to everyone?
notes.summary: Every month, find the most common customer problem, fix it with input from customers who succeeded anyway, test on struggling customers, then roll out — forever.

notes.title: More, Better, New: putting the Core Four on steroids
questions: My business has plateaued, how do I get more leads from what I already do?
Should I add a new marketing channel or double down on the one I have?
Should I focus on doing more volume or improving conversion rates?
When is the right time to try a new platform or advertising method?
notes.summary: Any lead-getting activity can be boosted three ways: do more of it, do it better, or do it somewhere new — usually in that order.

notes.title: Order for going new: placement, platform, then Core Four activity
questions: My Instagram ads are maxed out, should I try YouTube or another ad format next?
What's the easiest next marketing channel to add after my first one works?
Should I expand to a new social platform or try new formats on my current one?
notes.summary: When more and better stop paying, expand in the order that gets the most leads for the least work: new placements, then new platforms, then a new Core Four activity.

notes.title: Dean Jackson's nine-word email to re-engage a warm list
questions: How do I wake up an old email list that hasn't heard from me in a while?
What simple email can I send past leads to find out who is still interested?
How do I reconnect with past customers without a big sales pitch?
notes.summary: A plain one-line question email that surfaces which people on a warm list are currently interested.

notes.title: Offer, leads, sales: the three pieces needed to make money
questions: My business isn't making money, where do I start figuring out what's wrong?
What are the basic pieces every business needs to make sales?
Should I fix my product, my marketing, or my selling first?
Why does getting customers matter more than having a perfect product?
notes.summary: To make money you need something to sell (an offer), people to sell it to (leads), and a way to get them to buy (sales); skipping straight to "make money" fails.

notes.title: The one-customer thought experiment
questions: How would I treat customers if I could only grow through word of mouth?
What team exercise helps us improve the customer experience?
How do I design onboarding so customers send all their friends?
notes.summary: Imagine you lost every customer but one and are banned from the Core Four — all future customers must come from that one customer. Design what you'd do.

notes.title: The one-page advertising plan
questions: I've read a lot about marketing, how do I turn it into a simple daily plan?
What should my daily marketing commitment look like as a solo owner?
When should I stop doing marketing myself and pay someone to do it?
How do I keep myself accountable for doing marketing every day?
notes.summary: A five-step, single-page plan (about five minutes to fill out) that turns everything into a daily advertising commitment and recycles it to hire help.

notes.title: Open to goal: work until you hit the outcome
questions: Should I set a daily activity target or a results target for my sales team?
I hit my 100 outreach messages a day, what's the next level?
How do I let salespeople set their own hours but still hit numbers?
What do I do when doing my best isn't getting enough customers?
aliases: work until the goal is hit
notes.summary: The step after the Rule of 100: instead of committing to a number of actions, commit to a number of outcomes and work until you reach them, however long it takes.

notes.title: Paid ads action checklist
questions: What do I need to decide before launching a paid ad campaign?
How do I turn running ads into a concrete weekly plan for my business?
How much should I spend and how many ads should I make to start?
notes.summary: A filled-in planning card for a paid-ads program, answering who/what/where/when/why/how/how much/how many/how long.

notes.title: How paid ads work: renting reach, winning on efficiency
questions: Do Facebook or Google ads actually work for small businesses?
Why are my ads not making money even though people see them?
How should I scale ads from a small audience to a bigger one?
Should I start with paid ads or other marketing first?
notes.summary: Paid ads rent another business's audience so you reach cold strangers one-to-many; reach is guaranteed, getting your money back is not, so the game is efficiency, not reach.

notes.title: Choosing a platform to advertise on
questions: Should I advertise on Facebook, Instagram, Google, LinkedIn or TikTok?
How do I choose where to run my first ads?
Which ad format should I start with, stories, feed or video ads?
When should I add another advertising platform?
notes.summary: Advertise first on a platform that passes four tests, and start with the ad placements your competitors already use.

notes.title: Targeting: lookalike audiences plus filters
questions: Who should I target with my Facebook ads to reach likely buyers?
How do I use my customer list to find similar people with ads?
How narrow should ad targeting be for a local business?
My ads reach lots of people but the wrong ones, how do I fix the audience?
notes.summary: Get the highest number of likely buyers to see your ad by seeding a lookalike audience with your best lists, then layering simple filters on top.

notes.title: Three phases of ad spend: track, lose, print money
questions: How much money should I expect to lose before ads become profitable?
My first ads lost money, should I stop or keep going?
What should I set up before spending any money on ads?
When is it safe to massively increase my ad spend?
notes.summary: Scale paid ads in three phases: set up tracking, accept a learning period of losses, then spend as much as capacity allows once it's profitable.

notes.title: Pay affiliates in product: 'sell three, get it free'
questions: Can I reward partners who send me customers with free product instead of cash?
How do I motivate small affiliates without paying big commissions?
What's a cheap way to reward people who sell my supplements or products?
notes.summary: Reward affiliate performance with your product: they value it at retail, it costs you only your cost.

notes.title: Eleven ways to increase perceived likelihood of achievement
questions: Prospects doubt my service will work for them, how do I make them believe?
What kinds of proof should I put on my sales page?
I have no reviews yet, how can I build credibility with new clients?
Should I add a guarantee or testimonials to my offer?
notes.summary: A checklist of proof elements that make prospects believe they will get the result, so more say yes.

notes.title: Place a $100 ad to get in the game
questions: I'm not tech savvy, how do I run my very first online ad?
How much should I spend on my first ever ad as a test?
I keep putting off ads because they seem complicated, where do I start?
notes.summary: Stop saying "I'm not techy" and place one real $100 ad on a platform today; the lesson is worth far more than the money.

notes.title: Prepay plus guarantee: weaponise your guarantee to get cash up front
questions: How do I get clients to pay in full upfront instead of monthly?
Should I offer a money-back guarantee to everyone or only some buyers?
How can I collect more cash upfront for my coaching or service program?
What do I say when someone asks for a payment plan?
notes.summary: Offer your guarantee only to people who pay in full up front, which gets more yeses and more cash.

notes.title: Problem-solution cycle: picking the problem a lead magnet should solve
questions: What problem should my free offer solve so people later buy my main service?
My freebie attracts lots of people who never buy, why?
How do I connect a free resource to my paid product?
How does a realtor or agency pick a small problem to solve for free?
notes.summary: Every solution reveals a new problem; pick a narrow, meaningful problem for the lead magnet whose solution exposes a problem your core offer solves for money.

notes.title: Puddles, ponds, lakes, oceans: narrow your content focus first
questions: What niche should my small local business focus on for social media content?
My general business content gets no views, should I narrow down?
When should I broaden my content to a wider audience?
notes.summary: Start content in a narrow niche you can own, then widen step by step as your track record grows.

notes.title: Qualify affiliates by getting them invested
questions: How do I find affiliates who actually follow through and sell?
Should I charge partners or resellers for training and certification?
Should affiliates have to buy my product before they can promote it?
My resellers sign up but never sell anything, what should I change?
notes.summary: Make potential affiliates invest — by becoming customers, paying for expert certification, or both — because those who pay pay attention, win faster and make more.

notes.title: Start charging when referrals start, then raise price every five customers
questions: When should I start charging after doing free work for my first clients?
How do I figure out what to charge for a new service?
How quickly should I raise my prices as I get more customers?
How do I create real urgency to buy without fake deadlines?
notes.summary: Referrals are the litmus test that you're good enough to charge; then step prices up every five customers.

notes.title: Ask for referrals as an offer (Dropbox, PayPal)
questions: Why don't my customers refer friends even though they're happy?
Should I give both the customer and their friend a reward for referring?
What makes customers comfortable recommending me to people they know?
How did Dropbox and PayPal grow through referral rewards?
notes.summary: Referral requests only work when treated like an offer that shows what the customer (and friend) gets for referring — and the referrer's risk must be outweighed by benefits.

notes.title: Why referrals are the best leads: higher LTGP, lower CAC, exponential
questions: Why are customers who come from referrals so valuable?
Is it worth investing in a referral program instead of more ads?
How much do referrals actually lower my cost to get customers?
Why does word of mouth grow faster than advertising?
notes.summary: Referred customers are worth more and cost less, and word of mouth grows exponentially while the Core Four grows linearly.

notes.title: Referral gift card promotion
questions: How can my gym or coaching business get members to bring friends?
Should I give customers a gift card to pass on to a friend?
What referral promotion creates urgency for the friend to sign up?
notes.summary: Give each customer a personalized, expiring gift card worth about a third of the program price to hand to a friend — it gives the referrer status and creates urgency.

notes.title: Referral growth equation: referral rate minus churn
questions: Why does my membership business stay flat even though people refer friends?
How do I know if word of mouth alone can grow my business?
I have to keep advertising just to stay the same size, why?
What referral and cancellation rates should a subscription business track?
notes.summary: Monthly % of customers referred minus monthly % of customers churned = monthly compounding growth rate from word of mouth alone.

notes.title: Give each outreach rep a fixed weekly lead allotment (about 70% of capacity)
questions: How many leads should I give each salesperson per week?
My sales reps waste leads, how do I make them work every one?
How do I set fair appointment quotas for a setter team?
notes.summary: Give each rep an explicit number of leads per week, a bit under their capacity, so they work every lead fully and can be held to absolute quotas.

notes.title: New to an outreach team: shadow the best rep, double their inputs, replicate before you iterate
questions: How should a new sales rep get good fast?
Should I change the sales script or follow the proven one first?
I'm new to cold calling, how much activity should I do compared to the top performer?
notes.summary: Newcomers make up for lack of skill with volume: copy the top performer exactly at twice their activity, and only innovate after beating their numbers.

notes.title: Get everyone the best customers' results (and guarantee on those actions)
questions: How do I get all my clients the results my best clients get?
What conditions should I put on my guarantee?
How do I design onboarding based on what successful customers did?
How can I raise average results across my coaching program?
notes.summary: Find the actions your best-result customers took, force new customers to repeat them, and make those actions the conditions of your guarantee.

notes.title: Retain attention with curiosity: lists, steps and stories
questions: People stop watching my videos after a few seconds, how do I keep them?
How should I structure a post or video after the opening hook?
Should I use a numbered list, a step by step, or a story in my content?
How do I keep readers curious until the end of an email?
notes.summary: Curiosity drives retention; embed unanswered questions (explicit or implied) using lists, steps and stories.

notes.title: Reverse your ad budget from your customer goal
questions: How much should I spend on ads each day once they're profitable?
How do I set a monthly ad budget based on how many clients I want?
My ads work but I'm scared to spend more, how do I decide the number?
notes.summary: Once ads break even or better, set spend by working backward from how many customers you want or can handle, padded 20% for falling efficiency.

notes.title: Rule of 100: 100 primary actions a day for 100 days
questions: How much marketing should I be doing every day to get customers?
How many outreach messages or posts a day are enough?
I'm doing a little marketing and getting nothing, how much more is needed?
What daily routine should a new business owner commit to for getting leads?
notes.summary: Do 100 primary advertising actions every day for 100 days straight and you will get more engaged leads — Hormozi's one promise.

notes.title: Don't confuse a sales problem with an advertising problem
questions: My ads bring good leads on the phone but nobody buys, is it the ads?
Should I stop running ads if calls aren't converting into sales?
How do I tell whether I have a marketing problem or a closing problem?
notes.summary: If engaged leads have the problem you solve and the money to pay but aren't buying, your ads work — you have a sales problem.

notes.title: Sell better customers to get more referrals
questions: Should I stop selling to customers who aren't a good fit?
How do I attract more clients like my best ones?
My churn is high, should I change who I target?
How can targeting a narrower customer type increase referrals?
notes.summary: Find what your most successful customers have in common, target only people like them, and you raise product results, goodwill and referrals at once.

notes.title: Tell customers what to buy next
questions: What should I offer customers after they finish my program?
Customers drop off after their first purchase, how do I keep them buying?
How do I get repeat business from people who already love my product?
notes.summary: Customers who love your product want more; if you don't sell them the next thing, someone else will — and every extra product is another thing they can refer friends to.

notes.title: Seven ways to ask for referrals
questions: How do I ask customers for referrals without it feeling awkward?
How much should I pay customers for referring a friend?
When is the best moment to ask a new client for referrals?
Can I offer a discount in exchange for introductions during a sales call?
What referral rewards work if I don't want to pay cash?
notes.summary: A referral program has three components — how you give the incentive, what you incentivize with, and how you ask; these seven combinations worked best for Hormozi.

notes.title: Six ways to get more referrals by giving more value
questions: How do I make customers happy enough to refer people without asking?
What parts of my business should I improve to get more word of mouth?
Should I fix my product or start a referral program first?
notes.summary: Build referral-generating goodwill with six value levers that mirror the parts of an ad: call-out, the four value drivers, and the CTA.

notes.title: Size-of-the-pie fallacy: you haven't saturated your market
questions: I think I've saturated my local market, is there really room to grow?
Will spending more on ads exhaust my audience on the platform?
There are already several competitors doing the same ads, have I hit my ceiling?
notes.summary: Owners mistake the tiny slice of the market they reach — one channel, one platform, one style — for the whole market, and then think they've maxed out.

notes.title: Better beliefs about talent: everyone is replaceable
questions: I feel like nobody can do the work as well as I can, how do I let go?
Why does my business stay small when I do everything myself?
My staff never meet my standards, is it them or me?
How do I replace myself in my own business?
notes.summary: Replace "if you want it done right, do it yourself" with beliefs that let others outperform you — owners who compete with their team stay small.

notes.title: Train lead getters with the 3Ds: document, demonstrate, duplicate
questions: How do I train a new employee to do my job as well as I do?
How do I write a checklist or SOP someone else can follow?
How long should I give a new hire to prove themselves?
My trainee keeps making mistakes, how should I give feedback?
notes.summary: Turn a task you already do into a checklist, show it, then have the trainee do it in front of you, fixing the checklist until a stranger could get your results from it alone.

notes.title: Two ways to grow a business and four ways to improve leads
questions: What are the only ways a business can actually grow?
Should I focus on getting more customers or making each one worth more?
How do I avoid depending on a single source of customers?
aliases: more customers or more per customer
notes.summary: A business grows in only two ways, more customers or more value per customer, and you get more customers through more, better and cheaper leads, obtained reliably.

notes.title: Advertising is an inputs-outputs game: volume decides
questions: I reached out to a hundred people and got one client, does outreach not work?
How many flyers or mailers do I need to send to judge if it works?
Why do I get so few leads even though I'm doing marketing?
notes.summary: Most people dramatically underestimate the volume advertising needs; the right action in the wrong amount still fails, so input enough effort to get a readable output.

notes.title: Warm vs. cold audiences
questions: What's the difference between marketing to people who know me and strangers?
Should I treat my email list differently from a bought contact list?
Why do strangers respond so much less than my existing contacts?
notes.summary: A warm audience has given you permission to contact them; a cold audience has not.

notes.title: Warm outreach benchmarks and money math
questions: What reply rate should I expect when messaging my personal contacts?
How many people do I need to contact to get one paying customer?
How much money can I realistically make just reaching out to people I know?
Few people reply to my messages, where in the process is it breaking?
notes.summary: Expected conversion rates for warm outreach, used to predict customers per 100 reach-outs.

notes.title: 'Do you know anyone?' offer script built from the value equation
questions: What should I say to friends about my new business without being pushy?
How do I ask my network for clients without directly selling to them?
What's a good one-line pitch for what my business does?
How do I offer free work in exchange for testimonials?
notes.summary: A fill-in-the-blank warm offer that asks whether they know someone who needs help, rather than asking them to buy, so it never feels pushy.

notes.title: Ten steps of warm outreach to get your first five customers
questions: How do I get my first five clients for a brand new business?
How do I use my phone contacts and social media friends to find customers?
What should my first message to an old contact say?
How do I follow up with people I reached out to who didn't reply?
notes.summary: A step-by-step process for turning your personal contacts into your first customers and referrals.

notes.title: Warm outreach: one-to-one contact with people who know you
questions: What's the cheapest way to find my first customers with no marketing budget?
Should I contact people I already know when starting a business?
When should I move beyond my personal network to find customers?
What do I need at minimum to start getting customers?
aliases: reaching out to friends and family
notes.summary: Warm outreach means personally contacting people who already know you; it's the cheapest, easiest and most reliable way to find your first customers, and most businesses skip it.

notes.title: Weekly split-test cadence: one test per platform per week
questions: How often should I run A/B tests on my ads and funnel?
Should I test several changes at once or one at a time?
How long should I keep trying to beat my current best ad before moving on?
How do I keep track of what my marketing tests taught me?
notes.summary: Run exactly one split test per platform per week, log every result, and move to the next constraint if you can't beat the control in four tries or one month.

notes.title: What-Who-When framework for ad copy
questions: What should I write in the body of my ad copy?
How do I come up with lots of different angles for my ads?
I'm not a good copywriter, how do I write ads that sell?
How do I show the pain of not buying without being negative?
notes.summary: Generate every reason someone should be interested by running the value elements (what) through the perspectives of people who give status (who) across past, present and future (when).

notes.title: Whisper, tease, shout: the launch sequence
questions: How should I build hype before launching a new product or book?
How often should I post about a launch as the date gets closer?
How do I get partners and affiliates excited to promote my launch?
When should I start teasing a new offer to my audience?
notes.summary: Launch anything — and activate affiliates — in three phases that mirror an ad: whisper (curiosity/call-out), tease (value), shout (call to action), with escalating frequency as launch day nears.

notes.title: White-label your lead magnets for affiliates
questions: How can partners give my free resources to their own customers?
Can I let affiliates put their logo on my guides and checklists?
What can I give affiliates to help them attract leads quickly?
notes.summary: Let affiliates rebrand lead magnets you already built for your audience and use them with theirs.

notes.title: 100 ways to offer one product, not 100 products
questions: Do I need to launch new products to grow, or can I sell what I have differently?
How can a personal trainer make more money without adding new services?
I only have one service; how do I create more options to sell?
Should I keep adding products or just change pricing and packaging?
notes.summary: Get as much as you can out of what you already have: it is less about having 100 products and more about having 100 ways to offer your product. "Simple scales, fancy fails."

notes.title: A/B upselling: ask which, not whether
questions: Instead of asking if they want to buy, what question should my staff ask?
How do I stop customers saying no when I ask if they want an add-on?
Should I give customers two options to choose from instead of a yes/no question?
How do I nudge first-time customers toward the option I want them to pick?
notes.summary: Instead of asking if they want to buy, ask which of two options they prefer; both answers are a sale.

notes.title: Fill money-model gaps with other people's products (affiliate offers)
questions: I have nothing else to sell my customers; can I sell other companies' products?
How do I earn more per client without building or delivering anything new?
Should a massage therapist or agency recommend partner products for a commission?
My business has just one offer; how do I add revenue with zero extra operations?
notes.summary: Sell someone else's product for a commission to add offers without building or delivering anything.

notes.title: Buy X, get Y free (attraction offer)
questions: Is giving free items better than offering a percentage discount?
How do I make a discount sound like free stuff without losing profit?
How can I get customers to prepay for six or twelve months of service?
Should I raise my prices before running a buy-one-get-one-free promotion?
Most of my customers only buy once; how do I make that one purchase bigger?
notes.summary: When customers buy something they get other things free; reframe a discount (or a full price) as free stuff, because free draws far more attention than a percentage off.

notes.title: Decoy offer (attraction offer)
questions: My lead costs keep rising; how do I advertise something cheap that leads to a premium sale?
How do I run a free or $1 trial ad and still sell my expensive package?
Should I create a stripped-down cheap version to sit next to my premium service?
Why are people taking my cheap option instead of my best package?
aliases: free vs premium side by side
notes.summary: Advertise a free or cheap stripped-down version; when leads engage, present it side by side with a far more valuable premium offer and steer them to the premium.

notes.title: Giveaways (attraction offer)
questions: How do I run a contest that turns entrants into paying customers afterwards?
Can a dentist give away free braces to generate leads?
What do I offer everyone who entered my contest but didn't win?
Nobody entered my giveaway; what went wrong?
Are raffles and sweepstakes legal to use for marketing my business?
notes.summary: Advertise a chance to win a big prize in exchange for contact details and other information; after picking a winner, offer everyone else the prize at a discount.

notes.title: Attraction offers: turn advertising into customers with free or discounted offers
questions: How do I turn ad clicks into paying customers using a free or cheap first offer?
I spend too much getting customers and make too little up front; what should I fix first?
How can giving something away for free actually make me money?
Is offering something free better than offering a discount or a $1 deal?
notes.summary: Attraction offers generate leads and convert them into customers by offering something free or discounted, then make money on what comes with or after it.

notes.title: Pay less now or pay more later (attraction offer)
questions: How do I offer a risk-free trial where they pay only if satisfied?
Should I let people pay full price later or a discounted price today?
How do I get a card on file for a free workshop or event?
Too many trial users are cancelling before the bill; what should I change?
notes.summary: Let people choose between paying full price later (card on file, cancel if not satisfied and qualified) or paying a discounted price now with extra bonuses.

notes.title: Turn attraction offers into continuity with automatic renewal
questions: What happens when a customer's prepaid package ends; can it roll into monthly billing?
How do I turn a bulk prepaid deal into ongoing monthly revenue?
Should my six-month package auto-renew month to month afterwards?
notes.summary: Let bulk or prepaid attraction offers roll automatically into a month-to-month subscription when they end, getting attraction and continuity benefits from one offer.

notes.title: Win your money back (attraction offer)
questions: Should I offer customers their money back if they hit their goal?
How do I run a fitness challenge where people earn a refund by following the plan?
Will a money-back-for-results offer cost me too much in refunds?
How do I sell a program to people who keep starting and quitting things?
notes.summary: "If you do X or achieve Y within Z days, you get it free": customers pay up front and earn the money back (cash or store credit) by hitting tracked actions, results or both.

notes.title: Bam Fam: book a meeting from a meeting
questions: How do I get clients to keep coming back for appointments?
Should I book the next session before the client leaves?
My patients don't rebook; what should my front desk do at checkout?
notes.summary: End every appointment by scheduling the next one; more meetings mean more upsell opportunities and more people upsold.

notes.title: Barter: trade a discount for reviews, testimonials and referrals
questions: A good prospect says it's too expensive; can I give a discount in exchange for reviews?
How do I get testimonials and referrals from new clients when I'm just starting out?
Is it okay to discount if the customer gives me something in return?
notes.summary: On a price objection, offer a discount in exchange for advertising that is worth more to you than the discount costs.

notes.title: Bill every four weeks instead of monthly (+8.3% revenue)
questions: Should I charge members every four weeks instead of once a month?
How can I increase subscription revenue without getting new customers?
Is there an easy billing change that raises yearly profit on memberships?
notes.summary: A year has 13 four-week cycles but only 12 months; billing $100 every four weeks instead of $100 a month gets the same buyers and 8.3% more annual revenue.

notes.title: Billing cadence affects churn: annual 2%, quarterly 5%, monthly 10.7%
questions: Do annual plans have lower cancellation rates than monthly plans?
Members keep cancelling; should I push quarterly or yearly billing?
In what order should I present annual, quarterly and monthly prices?
Does how often I bill customers affect how long they stay?
notes.summary: Subscription data from about 14,000 businesses (reported by ProfitWell) showed that less frequent billing goes with much lower monthly cancellation.

notes.title: $100M Money Models in one page (book recap)
questions: What are all the ways to make more money from each customer, in one list?
Give me a quick summary of every offer type for increasing sales per customer.
What short scripts can I use for each step of selling more to buyers?
notes.summary: The whole book as a checklist: the purpose of a money model, its standards, and the 15 named offers with their one-line scripts.

notes.title: Bulk prepay upsell on continuity: 1 in 8 lifts 30-day profit 50%
questions: Right after someone joins monthly, should I offer a discount to prepay several months?
How do I collect more cash in the first month from new members?
What's a good deal to get monthly members to pay for five or six months up front?
notes.summary: Once someone joins month to month, offer a discount for prepaying a block of months; a small take rate raises 30-day cash a lot.

notes.title: Fast cash from existing customers (and keep selling prepaid buyers)
questions: My recurring business needs cash fast; how do I raise it from current customers?
Should I keep selling to customers who already prepaid for a year?
How many existing members should I let prepay without hurting monthly cash flow?
notes.summary: Offer current recurring customers a prepay deal ("buy 10, get 2 free" at their current rate), capped at about 10% of the base, and keep making offers to people who prepay.

notes.title: Cancellation policy: the fee equals the discount they received
questions: What should I charge if a customer breaks their contract early?
How do I set a fair cancellation policy for discounted long-term plans?
Should I make it easy for customers to cancel?
Do strict cancellation terms reduce sign-ups?
notes.summary: Decide cancellation terms up front; Hormozi's favourite is that cancelling early costs exactly the discount the customer received for committing.

notes.title: Card on file: "Want to just use the card on file?"
questions: How do I make it easier for existing customers to buy add-ons?
Should my staff ask to charge the card we already have saved?
Customers hesitate at checkout when paying again; how do I reduce that friction?
notes.summary: Ask whether they want to use the card you already have instead of asking them to pay; it removes the hidden costs of buying.

notes.title: Bad money models kill businesses: the slow-payback trap
questions: My customers are profitable over time but I can't afford to keep running ads; why?
I keep running out of cash even though my business is profitable on paper.
Why do I have to stop advertising every time the month ends in the red?
Is it a problem if it takes two years to earn back what I spent getting a customer?
notes.summary: When it costs more to get a customer than the first purchase earns, the business starves for cash even if lifetime profit is high.

notes.title: 30-day payback and the "one customer pays for two" standard
questions: How quickly should a new customer pay back what I spent to acquire them?
How do I make customers fund my ad spend within the first month?
Can I use a credit card to pay for ads and repay it from new sales?
What's a good target for first-month profit versus acquisition cost?
notes.summary: Cover the cost of getting (and serving) a customer within 30 days; a $100M money model goes further and funds at least two more customers from each one in that window.

notes.title: Customer value compounds: 2x value grows the business 8x
questions: Should I focus on cheaper leads or on making each customer worth more?
How much faster can I grow if each customer spends twice as much?
Why does increasing customer value grow the business so much?
notes.summary: Making each customer more valuable, faster, compounds: you can afford more customers and recycle cash sooner.

notes.title: Continuity bonus offer: an awesome thing if they sign up today
questions: What can I give away free to get people to sign up for my monthly plan today?
How do I advertise a subscription without just saying 'join my membership'?
What bonuses work well for a gym, newsletter or subscription box sign-up?
How do I turn challenge or trial customers into monthly members?
notes.summary: Give a bonus worth more than the first continuity payment to anyone who joins today; advertise the bonus, not the membership.

notes.title: Continuity discount offer: free time if they commit today
questions: How do I get customers to commit to a year instead of month to month?
Should I give free months at the start or at the end of a contract?
If I give three months free with a year, how many months should they pay?
Competitors sell month to month; how do I get longer commitments?
notes.summary: Give products or service time free in exchange for committing to a longer paid term (buy X, get Y free, continuity style); decide how you apply the discount and your cancellation policy.

notes.title: Continuity offers: sell once, get paid again and again (and make them last)
questions: Should I sell my product as a one-time price or a monthly subscription?
Does it make sense to start my business with only a membership offer?
How do I get paid every month instead of once per customer?
When should I introduce a monthly plan in my sales process?
notes.summary: Continuity offers give ongoing value for ongoing payments until the customer cancels; they attract more buyers than a big one-time price but collect less cash now, so Hormozi offers them last in the sequence.

notes.title: Pricing the one-time option vs continuity: the 1.33x to 2.66x table
questions: How should I price a one-time option next to my monthly membership?
How much more will people pay to avoid a recurring commitment?
I want more people on the monthly plan; how high should the one-time price be?
notes.summary: Offer a higher one-time price alongside continuity; the bigger the one-time price relative to the monthly rate, the more people choose continuity.

notes.title: Waived fee offer: month to month with a big setup fee, or commit and it's waived
questions: Should I charge a setup fee for month-to-month clients and waive it for annual contracts?
How do I keep high-ticket clients from quitting before results show up?
How big should a setup fee be for an SEO or agency retainer?
What should a client pay if they leave a 12-month commitment early?
notes.summary: Offer month to month with a startup fee of 3 to 5x the monthly rate, or waive the fee for a 12+ month commitment; cancelling early means paying the waived fee.

notes.title: Presenting a decoy offer: "Free stuff or lasting results?"
questions: A lead came in for the free offer; how do I pitch them the paid package?
What do I say to steer prospects from the cheap option to the better one?
How do I close confidently without hype once they choose the premium?
notes.summary: Get permission to present the premium first, contrast it with the decoy, let the prospect choose the premium themselves, then assume the close.

notes.title: Use a $1 trial instead of free to justify the card on file
questions: People won't give a card for a free trial; should I charge a dollar instead?
Is a $1 first month better than a free trial for subscriptions?
How do I make sure the card works before recurring billing starts?
notes.summary: Some people resist giving a card for something free; a tiny price (first month for $1, then $X/month) justifies the card and confirms it works before recurring billing starts.

notes.title: Feature downsell: take something away, lower the price, ask "How about now?"
questions: A customer says it's too expensive; what can I remove instead of cutting the price?
How do I offer a cheaper version without discounting my main service?
Should I negotiate when a customer wants the same thing for less?
What can I offer someone who wants to pay less overall, not just later?
notes.summary: Lower the price by changing what customers get (less quantity, lower quality, cheaper alternatives, or removing components), never by discounting the same thing.

notes.title: Downsell offers and the rules of downselling
questions: What should I offer a customer after they say no?
Is it wrong to just drop my price when someone says it's too expensive?
How do I recover sales from people who turn down my main offer?
Should I plan my backup offers before the sales call?
notes.summary: A downsell is any offer made after someone says no; it tweaks how they pay or what they get to find the highest-value solution within their budget, never the same thing for less.

notes.title: Payment plan downsell: seven steps from paid-in-full to free trial
questions: A customer says they can't afford it right now; what payment options should I offer?
How do I split payments without losing cash flow?
Should I add interest for paying over time or discount paying in full?
Should I offer financing, layaway or 'half now, half on payday'?
notes.summary: "It costs too much" usually means "it costs too much right now"; spread the same price over time, stepping down from most cash up front to least, and stop as soon as they buy.

notes.title: Trial with penalty: free if they do the work, a fee if they don't
questions: Should I let hesitant prospects start free if they agree to do the work?
How do I offer a free trial that doesn't attract freeloaders?
Can I charge a fee to trial users who skip onboarding or check-ins?
How do I get software customers to actually complete onboarding?
notes.summary: Let people who said no start free on condition they do what makes customers successful; if they skip the requirements, they pay a fee.

notes.title: The Economist play: sell both by pricing the bundle like one option
questions: How do I get customers to buy two products together instead of the cheaper one?
How should I price a bundle next to single options?
Customers only pick the digital version; how do I sell print plus digital?
notes.summary: To get people to buy two products together, offer A, B and A+B, with A+B priced the same as the more expensive single option.

notes.title: Example: Boot Factory's "buy one pair, get two free"

My customers are tourists who buy once; how do I make that sale bigger?
Can I triple my price and give extra items free so the ad says free?
notes.summary: A Nashville boot store tripled the price of a pair and gave two more away, turning a fair price into a free offer.

notes.title: Example: burger upsell math (25 cents to $3 profit)

Is it okay if my first product barely makes money?
What's my version of asking 'do you want fries with that'?
notes.summary: A $2 burger earning $0.25 profit becomes a $3 profit order through three upsells, showing the first offer need not be profitable.

notes.title: Example: how not to downsell (the insurance that dropped from $5,000 to $400)

Why do customers stop trusting me after I cut my price on the spot?
What should a salesperson offer instead of cutting the price of the same add-on?

notes.title: Example: making the challenge free for members tripled membership sales
questions: Should I give my paid challenge free to people who become members?
How did a gym get more challenge buyers to join as monthly members?

notes.summary: A gym marketing six-week challenges started offering the challenge free to anyone who became a member, plus member-only bonuses, then upsold a prepaid six months.

notes.title: Example: the gym client who invented win-your-money-back (13 referrals)

A prospect wants accountability but won't buy; what deal could I offer them?

notes.title: Example: removing the guarantee tripled close rate (25% to 75%)

What happens if I let price objectors pay less but drop the guarantee?
Does taking away my guarantee make customers value it more and pay full price?
notes.summary: A high-ticket seller offered a cheaper price without the money-back guarantee; many then chose full price to keep the guarantee.

notes.title: Example: full-ride scholarship giveaway for a fitness certification
questions: How did a certification company use a free scholarship to fill its program?
Can a course or coaching business give one free spot and sell the rest at a discount?
How do I make a discounted price feel like a big win for applicants?
notes.summary: A fitness-certification company got tons of engaged leads by advertising one full-ride scholarship and then offering partial scholarships to everyone else.

notes.title: Example: free earmuffs that sell $30 storage
questions: Can a free gift create a need for something I sell?
How did a store charge customers to store a free item it gave them?
Can giving away a freebie with a service lead to a paid add-on sale?
notes.summary: A fur-coat dealer advertised free earmuffs with coat storage, then charged to store the earmuffs and closed with a question designed to get a "no".

notes.title: Example: Gym Launch's money model, built in layers to $4.4M a month
questions: How did a B2B coaching company grow to millions a month by adding offers one at a time?
What does a full sales sequence look like for a consulting business selling to gym owners?
When should I add the next offer to my business?
notes.summary: How Gym Launch went from one decoy offer to $4.4M/month in 20 months by adding one offer layer at a time.

notes.title: Example: opening gyms full on day one ($1 in, $34 out in 48 hours)

How did a gym fill up before opening using a cheap first program?
notes.summary: Hormozi's early gym launches pre-sold an empty building and used the cash to build it out, a money model that a famous marketer called a "level 10 skill set" in a "level 2 opportunity".

notes.title: Example: the HR software that waived onboarding if you did the training
questions: Can making customers finish training reduce churn for my software?

notes.summary: An HR software company won Hormozi's business (100+ employees at Gym Launch) by waiving its onboarding fee for customers who completed the training, and charging those who skipped it.

notes.title: Example: the $19 rental car that became $100 a day

notes.summary: A rental-car counter turned a $19/day booking into about $100/day (5x) with five well-timed offers, each solving a problem the customer had or would have.

notes.title: Example: the rollover that fixed Hormozi's zero-recurring-revenue gym
questions: My customers leave after their program ends and I have no recurring revenue; what fixes that?

notes.summary: His win-your-money-back program sold well but left him with no recurring revenue, until a friend showed him how to roll winnings into a year-long membership.

notes.title: Example: "double your reading speed in three hours or it's free"
questions: How can a trainer get paid for a free workshop without a sales pitch?
What's an example of 'pay later if it works' for a training session?
Does offering a cheaper pay-now price next to a pay-if-satisfied option work?
notes.summary: A speed-reading trainer offered a free training with two payment options, earning $297 from Hormozi without pitching during the session.

notes.title: Example: the "free" storage month that earns $127
questions: How can a storage facility profit from giving the first month free?
What can I sell right after a customer takes my free offer?
How do I make money if my first offer is free?
notes.summary: A storage-facility owner advertised a free first month yet collected about $127 from each new renter by selling everything the free unit made them need.

notes.title: Example: the $16,000 suit that sold a $2,200 suit
questions: How did a tailor get a customer to spend five times his budget?
Should I show my most expensive item first to make the main one look cheap?
How can a clothing shop get customers to spend well over their budget happily?

notes.title: Example: how Hormozi learned to sell supplements (A/B, prescription, unselling)

notes.summary: Three accidents across three years produced the four menu-upsell tactics, taking supplement sales from zero to tens of thousands per launch.

notes.title: Example: the $5 five-day tanning pass and the "turkey talk"
questions: How did a tanning salon turn $5 passes into monthly memberships?
How do I explain to customers that results take longer than they expect?

notes.summary: A tanning salon sold a $5, five-day VIP pass, then converted pass holders into $19.99/month memberships; Hormozi later adapted the idea into the decoy offer that saved his gyms.

notes.title: Example: a year of free trash hauling for a five-year contract
questions: Is it worth giving a full year free to win a five-year commercial contract?
How do I survive cash flow when I give new contracts a free first period?
Can a B2B service win big accounts by offering the first year free?
notes.summary: A neighbour built and sold a commercial trash business by offering big apartment complexes a full year of free service if they signed five paid years.

notes.title: Exit interviews: waive the cancellation fee to earn a save conversation
questions: A member wants to cancel; how do I try to save them?
Should I waive the cancellation fee if they come in and talk to me?
What do I say to an angry customer who is leaving?
notes.summary: When someone wants to cancel, ask for an exit interview (offer to waive the cancellation fee for it), let them vent, and solve or upgrade.

notes.title: Proactively downsell customers who aren't using features
questions: Should I offer a cheaper plan to clients who aren't using everything they pay for?
How do I stop subscribers cancelling because they don't use all the features?
Is it smart to lower a customer's bill before they ask?
notes.summary: When a customer is not using a feature they pay for, offer a lower price for only what they use, before they cancel.

notes.title: Checklist of service features you can dial down (or up)
questions: What parts of my service can I cut to make a cheaper package?
How do I create good, better and best tiers for a service business?
What can I add to a premium tier to justify a higher price?
notes.summary: A menu of service dimensions to remove or reduce in a feature downsell, or to raise in a premium tier.

notes.title: The four types of offers in a money model
questions: What kinds of offers should every business have to maximize revenue per customer?
How do I audit where my business is leaving money on the table?
In what order should I build my sales offers?
notes.summary: Money models combine four offer types: attraction (get customers), upsell (sell the next thing), downsell (sell something when they say no) and continuity (get paid again and again).

notes.title: Four ways to frame the same discount
questions: Is '25% off' or '$300 off' or '3 months free' better for my promotion?
How should I word a discount in my ad?
Should I advertise free months or a lower total price?
notes.summary: The same discount can be stated four ways; test which converts best in your market.

notes.title: Free orientation as a bridge to a DIY downsell
questions: Someone refused all my done-for-you packages; what can I still offer them?
How do I make money from prospects who won't hire me?
Should a service business invite non-buyers to a free orientation?
notes.summary: When someone refuses all your done-for-you options, invite them to a free orientation and offer a do-it-yourself product at the end.

notes.title: Free offers get more leads; discount offers get more shows
questions: Lots of leads book but don't show up; should I stop offering it free?
Should my clinic offer a free consultation or a small paid one?
Does charging a little reduce no-shows for appointments?
notes.summary: A free attraction offer brings more leads, while a discounted one brings fewer leads but a higher show-up rate.

notes.title: The gift card play: sell $200 gift cards for $20, then roll them over
questions: Can I sell discounted gift cards as a holiday promotion to bring in new clients?
How do I get customers to pay to refer their friends?
How big should a gift card be compared to what I sell next?
notes.summary: Advertise gift cards at 90% off, usable only by someone else; when the recipient comes in, roll the card's value into a bigger offer.

notes.title: Giveaway scarcity and urgency: cap entries, deadline to enter, claim and use
questions: How long should my contest run and how many entries should I allow?
How do I get contest winners to claim their prize quickly?
My team can't call all the contest entrants; how should I limit it?
notes.summary: Limit a giveaway by time and number of entries, and put a deadline on each step: entering, claiming and using.

notes.title: Pricing the giveaway promotional offer: small discount, big value gap
questions: How much should I discount for people who entered my contest but didn't win?
How do I make a small discount feel like a big saving?
What price should the runner-up offer be in a scholarship promotion?
notes.summary: Keep the actual discount small (rule of thumb 10 to 30% of gross margin) and frame it against the grand prize's stated value.

notes.title: Refer a winner: two prizes for twice the leads
questions: How do I get contest entrants to refer their friends?
Should I give a prize to whoever referred the winner?
How can a giveaway spread by word of mouth without attracting low-quality entrants?
notes.summary: Tell entrants that if someone they refer wins the grand prize, they win one too; referrals multiply and stay high quality.

notes.title: Hint at your next offer early in events and consultations
questions: Should I mention my next program at the start of a workshop or webinar?
How do I make people want my paid offer before I pitch it?
Few people buy at the end of my presentation; how do I prime them earlier?
notes.summary: Mention early on that people always ask about your next offer and that you will cover it at the end; it primes demand so more people buy when you finally offer it.

notes.title: The hyper-buying cycle: sell more when they are buying more
questions: When are customers most willing to buy many things at once?
Should I sell more to people who just started a new hobby, moved or had a baby?
My business serves weddings; should I worry about offering too many extras?
notes.summary: When people start something new they enter a short window of peak excitement in which they spend a large amount quickly; keep making offers then.

notes.title: Integrate upsells into what you deliver
questions: How do I get customers to ask for my add-ons instead of me pitching them?
My extra products feel like a cold sales pitch; how do I fix that?
Should I mention my other products inside my course or onboarding materials?
notes.summary: Build what you want to sell next into how you deliver the first thing, so customers ask for it.

notes.title: Lifetime discount at your most common churn point
questions: Most subscribers cancel around month four; how do I get them past that point?
Should I reward long-term subscribers with a lower price for life?
How do I reduce churn at the month people usually quit?
notes.summary: Advertise a lifetime lower rate that customers earn by staying past the month when most people cancel.

notes.title: The magnetic middle: price a third option to move buyers up
questions: How should I price small, medium and large to sell more of the large?
Most customers buy my smallest package; how do I move them up?
When should I raise prices on all my tiers?
notes.summary: With small, medium and large options, set the middle price to push the undecided toward the size you want.

notes.title: Make everyone a winner: upsell mid-program and let the losers win
questions: What do I offer challenge participants who didn't hit their goal?
When should I pitch my long-term program during a short challenge?
How do I keep people who fail a program from leaving?
notes.summary: Sell the program as if only qualifiers get their money back, then privately credit everyone toward the long-term offer, whether or not they hit the goal.

notes.title: Make your own money model in four steps
questions: Where do I start building a sales sequence for my business?
What offer should I add first, second and third to grow revenue?
How do I plan my pricing and offers step by step as a bootstrapped owner?
notes.summary: Add one offer type at a time, in order: attraction, upsell, downsell, continuity, each with a specific goal.

notes.title: Give members status titles as a bonus
questions: What free perk can I give long-term members?
Do loyalty levels like silver, gold and diamond keep members longer?
I can't think of a bonus for my membership that costs nothing; any ideas?
notes.summary: Award titles at milestones (3, 6, 12+ months: silver, gold, diamond, double diamond); customers can come to value the title more than the perks.

notes.title: There are no rules: mix and match offer types
questions: Do I have to follow the offers in a set order?
My business doesn't fit the usual sales sequence; can I change the order?
Can I use a monthly subscription as the first thing I sell to new customers?
notes.summary: Offers can be used anywhere in the sequence: upsell tactics in attraction offers, a downsell process behind every offer, continuity to attract.

notes.title: Money model: a deliberate sequence of offers
questions: How do I make more from each customer, faster?
How do I make several offers to a customer without feeling pushy?
What's the minimum a new customer should be worth in the first 30 days?
How do I review whether my business makes enough per customer?
notes.summary: A money model is a deliberate sequence of offers (what you offer, when, and how) designed to increase how many customers you get, how much they pay and how fast they pay it.

notes.title: Ground rules for using money models ethically and effectively
questions: Should I refund a customer who asks even if they don't qualify?
Is it ethical to use aggressive promotions like free offers or penalties?
Will these sales tactics work in my type of business?
Do I need a lawyer before advertising something as free?
notes.summary: Seven principles Hormozi sets before teaching any offer.

notes.title: Name your feature combinations, and call the cheapest "the minimum"
questions: What should I name my service packages?
How do I close someone who rejects every package I offer?
Should my cheapest package have a special name?
notes.summary: Pre-built, named packages close more; name the top one after an aspirational status and the bottom one "the minimum".

notes.title: Check that payment plans add buyers, not cannibalize paid-in-full
questions: Are payment plans stealing customers who would have paid in full?
How do I know if offering installments is actually helping sales?
Fewer people pay up front since we added financing; is that a problem?
notes.summary: After adding payment plans, total close rate should rise while the share of prospects paying in full stays the same.

notes.title: Payment-plan upsells and fewer declined payments
questions: Too many recurring payments fail; how do I recover declined cards?
Should I offer a pay-off discount to customers on installment plans?
What day should I charge customers to avoid failed payments?
notes.summary: Periodically re-offer the original paid-in-full discount to people on plans, and align charges with paydays to cut declines.

notes.title: Perfect one offer at a time; measure in quarters
questions: Should I launch all my new offers at once?
How long should I test one offer before adding another?
I'm trying to fix pricing, offers and subscriptions together and it's chaos; what now?
notes.summary: Do not implement a whole money model at once; get one offer working reliably, then automatic, before adding the next.

notes.title: Add a 3% processing fee, and waive it for a second payment method
questions: Should I add a credit card processing fee to my prices?
How do I get customers to give a backup payment method or bank debit?
Will customers refuse to buy because of a 3% surcharge?
notes.summary: Quote price plus a 3% processing fee, then offer to waive it if the customer provides a backup payment method (ideally ACH bank debit).

notes.title: Raise prices in stages: start cheap, raise until the nos outweigh the yeses
questions: How should I price a brand new offer?
When do I stop raising prices on my service?
Should I start cheap and raise prices as I get better?
notes.summary: Launch new offers cheap to get many yeses and feedback, improve the product, then keep raising price until the extra cash from yeses no longer makes up for the lost sales.

notes.title: Required check-ins: build upsell moments into the program
questions: How do I build natural selling moments into my coaching program?
Should check-in meetings be mandatory for clients in a challenge or trial?
When during a program should I offer the next service?
notes.summary: Make attendance at check-in meetings part of the qualifying criteria; each meeting helps the customer succeed and is a natural moment to make the next offer.

notes.title: Win-back campaigns: roll past spend into a return offer
questions: How do I bring back old customers who haven't bought in six months?
What offer gets lapsed clients to return?
Can I get competitors' unhappy customers to switch to me?
notes.summary: Contact customers 6+ months since their last purchase and offer to credit part of what they spent before toward something new.

notes.title: Seesaw downselling: a simpler payment-plan script
questions: What's a simple payment script for new salespeople on high-ticket sales?
How do I get prospects to put more money down up front?
How do I handle 'the monthly payment is too high'?
notes.summary: For fewer steps or newer salespeople, frame monthly payments as the bad option and let the prospect trade a bigger down payment for smaller monthly payments.

notes.title: Sell guarantees, warranties and insurance instead of giving them away
questions: Should I charge for a warranty I currently give away for free?
Can I sell damage protection or insurance as an add-on?
How much should an extended warranty cost compared to the product price?
notes.summary: If you already provide a guarantee, warranty or replacement policy for free, offer it as a paid add-on at about 5 to 50% of the price.

notes.title: Surprise and delight: give every bonus even if they said yes early
