questions: If a customer says yes before I mention all the bonuses, do they still get them?
How do I avoid customers feeling cheated when they compare deals?
Should I hold back extras to win over undecided buyers, and give them to everyone?
notes.summary: If you hold bonuses to tip fence-sitters, add them one at a time; if someone says yes before you reach them all, still give them every bonus.

notes.title: The 1-to-10 temperature check
questions: How do I know if a prospect has a money problem or doesn't really want it?
What question do I ask when a customer keeps rejecting payment options?
When should I stop offering payment plans and change the package?
notes.summary: After two rejected downsells (or when money seems tight), ask how badly they want it on a scale of 1 to 10, and route the sale by the answer.

notes.title: Three stages of a money model: get cash, get more cash, get the most cash
questions: What should I work on first: getting customers, selling more, or recurring revenue?
Why does my business break when sales start working?
How do I know which growth stage my business is at?
aliases: get cash, more cash, most cash
notes.summary: Build money models in stages that each pay for the next: attraction offers (get cash), upsells and downsells (get more cash), continuity (get the most cash).

notes.title: Anchor upsell: show the premium first, then come to the rescue
questions: Should I show customers a very expensive option first?
How do I make my main package look affordable?
Is it worth offering a premium version even if few buy it?
What if a customer has a bigger budget than my standard offer?
notes.summary: Present a premium version 5 to 10 times the price of your main offer first; when the customer gasps, offer the main offer as the relief.

notes.title: The classic upsell: "You can't have X without Y"
questions: What can I sell right after someone's first purchase?
How do I get customers to spend more per order?
I only sell one product; what should I offer next?
When is the best moment to offer an add-on?
notes.summary: Offer the solution to the customer's next problem the moment they become aware of it; current customers buy far more readily than strangers, and when timed right they upsell themselves.

notes.title: Upselling from a trial: they like it, hate it, or don't use it
questions: What should I say to trial users who love it, hate it, or never use it?
How do I turn unhappy trial users into paying customers?
Should I bill trial users who never started?
notes.summary: Every trial user falls into one of three groups; meet each and make a tailored next offer.

notes.title: Menu upsell: "You don't need that, you need this"
questions: How do I recommend products during a consultation without sounding salesy?
Should I tell customers which products they don't need?
How do I sell add-ons when I have many products to choose from?
Can I sell items that are out of stock?
notes.summary: Tell customers which options they do not need (unsell), prescribe exactly what they do need and how to use it, ask which variant they prefer (A/B), and make paying easy (card on file).

notes.title: Upsell offers: whatever you offer next
questions: Why aren't my customers buying my add-ons?
What should I offer customers after their first purchase?
Where does most of the profit come from in a business with low-margin products?
notes.summary: An upsell is simply whatever you offer next; every solution reveals a new problem, and you sell the solution to the problem your last offer revealed.

notes.title: Rollover upsell: credit what they already paid toward the next offer
questions: Can I credit what a customer already paid toward a bigger package?
Instead of a refund, what can I offer an unhappy customer?
How much credit should I give toward a bigger purchase?
How do I turn a short first purchase into a 12-month commitment?
notes.summary: Credit some or all of a customer's previous purchase toward a bigger offer; in Hormozi's experience far more people take it.

notes.title: How to set win-your-money-back criteria
questions: What conditions should customers meet to earn a refund?
How do I set conditions for a guarantee that customers can't game?
What should trial users have to do to avoid being charged?
notes.summary: Good refund criteria are easy to track, likely to produce the customer's result, and advertise the business; they make or break the offer.

notes.title: "You don't want anything else, do you?": get a no that means yes
questions: What should I ask at the end of a sale so 'no' confirms the purchase?
What's a closing line where 'no' still means they buy?
How do I word the last question at the register so customers keep the add-on?
notes.summary: People are trained to answer "You don't want anything else, do you?" with "no", so phrase the close so that "no" confirms the purchase you just offered.

notes.title: Agency moves from retainer to pay-for-performance: 22.4x cash upfront
questions: My marketing agency charges a monthly retainer and loses money on ads upfront; what should change?
Can switching an agency from retainer to getting paid only on results really increase revenue?
How much more cash can a better offer bring in from the same ad budget?
notes.summary: Worked numbers showing how a Grand Slam Offer multiplies response, close rate and price at the same ad spend (based on a lead-gen agency using one of Hormozi's software companies, rounded).

notes.title: Clean the pipeline with every price increase
questions: Should I tell my prospects before I raise my prices?
How do I raise prices without upsetting people who are still deciding?
Is there a way to turn a price increase into a quick burst of sales?
What's the best way to get fence-sitting leads to finally buy?
notes.summary: Before raising prices, tell every prospect in the pipeline that the price is going up so they can get in at the current rate.

notes.title: Anti-guarantee: all sales final, with a strong reason why
questions: Should I offer refunds on a digital product people can copy once they see it?
How do I tell buyers there are no refunds without scaring them off?
My high-ticket consulting is fully custom; can I make all sales final?
Can refusing to give a money-back guarantee actually help sales?
notes.summary: State plainly that all sales are final, and give a believable reason that shows your exposure.

notes.title: Arnold's charity fundraiser: cut supply, raise price, raise more
questions: Can raising the ticket price and selling fewer tickets bring in more money for an event?
How do I get donors or bidders to pay far more at a charity auction?
What happens if I cut supply when demand for my event is high?
notes.summary: At the After-School All-Stars fundraiser at Arnold Schwarzenegger's home, scarcity, urgency and bonuses made identical items sell for many times their normal price.

notes.title: Best case / worst case close
questions: What can I say when a prospect is scared the program won't work for them?
How do I close someone who keeps hesitating because of risk?
How do I use my refund promise during the closing conversation?
notes.summary: Pair a strong guarantee with a close that shows both outcomes are safe, and that only walking away is risky.

notes.title: Bonus presentation checklist (11 points)
questions: How should I describe each bonus on my sales page so it feels valuable?
Should I put a dollar value on every extra I include?
What kinds of extras do buyers value more, trainings or tools and checklists?
How much should my bonuses be worth compared to the main product?
How can bonuses answer the reasons a buyer thinks they'll fail?
notes.summary: Rules for building and presenting each bonus so it adds maximum perceived value.

notes.title: Add bonuses instead of discounting
questions: A customer asked me for a discount; what should I do instead?
How do I negotiate without dropping my price?
Should I ever cut my price to close a deal on a sales call?
notes.summary: When a prospect asks for a better deal, never cut the price of the core offer; add a bonus instead.

notes.title: Bonuses: stack components to widen the price-to-value gap
questions: Why do infomercials keep adding extras before revealing the price?
Should I sell my service as one package or list out every part?
How can I make my offer feel worth more without lowering the price?
Customers don't see everything I do for them; how do I make it visible?
notes.summary: An offer broken into named parts and presented as a stack of bonuses is perceived as more valuable than the same offer presented as one thing.

notes.title: $100M Offers in 11 steps (book recap checklist)
questions: What are the steps to build a great offer from start to finish?
I want to audit my current offer; what should I check, in order?
Is there a checklist for fixing a weak offer before spending on ads?
notes.summary: The whole book as a build sequence for a high-margin, decommoditized Grand Slam Offer.

notes.title: Brooke Castillo's 90-day relationship course: problems and solutions list
questions: How would a relationship or life coach build a program around client problems?
Does listing problems and turning them into solutions work outside fitness?
What problems should a 90-day dating or marriage coaching program solve?
notes.summary: Life coach Brooke Castillo applied the problems-to-solutions step to a 90-day relationship course, showing the method works far outside fitness.

notes.title: Charge far above cost, never above value
questions: I price by adding a markup to my costs; is that the wrong approach?
I feel guilty charging so much more than it costs me to deliver; should I?
How much higher than my costs can my price reasonably be?
What's the upper limit on what I can charge customers?
notes.summary: Aim to charge many times what delivery costs (Hormozi says think up to 100x, not 2-3x), as long as the buyer still gets more value than they pay.

notes.title: What makes a good bonus (and what to pull out of the core)
questions: What makes a good freebie to include with a purchase?
What cheap extras can I give away that customers still value highly?
Which parts of my program should I pull out and present as separate bonuses?
How do I build up a library of bonuses over time?
notes.summary: The best bonuses cost time or money to create once but can be given away endlessly, and feel like they could stand alone.

notes.title: Commodity vs category of one (price-driven vs value-driven purchases)
questions: Prospects keep comparing my quote to cheaper competitors; how do I stop that?
Customers think all providers in my industry are the same; what do I do?
How do I get people to buy on value instead of price?
Do I need to change my service to stand out, or just how I package it?
notes.summary: If buyers can compare you like-for-like they buy on price; differentiate the offer so they buy on value instead.

notes.title: Catalogue of conditional guarantees
questions: What guarantee can I offer that requires clients to actually do the work?
What can I promise besides a refund if a client doesn't get results?
How can a B2B service guarantee results without going broke on refunds?
Should I offer to keep working for free until the client hits their goal?
Can I delay a client's second payment until they see their first result?
notes.summary: Conditional guarantees attach terms, ideally the actions that produce success, and can be "better than money back".

notes.title: Divergent thinking for offer creation (the brick exercise)
questions: I'm stuck coming up with ideas for my offer; how do I brainstorm better?
Is there a warm-up exercise to get creative before designing a product?
Why is there no single right answer when designing an offer?
notes.summary: Offer building is a divergent problem: generate many possible solutions to one problem rather than converging on one right answer.

notes.title: The delicate dance of desire: leave demand unmet
questions: Should I sell every seat I can, or leave some people wanting more?
Is it better to sell a cheap group workshop or a few expensive one-on-one spots?
Why does each launch I run sell fewer spots than the last?
How do I keep demand high so I can raise prices over time?
notes.summary: Desire exists only while it is unsatisfied, so selling slightly less than demand keeps prospects hungry and lets you charge more over time.

notes.title: The delivery cube: ways to vary how a solution is delivered
questions: What different ways could I deliver my coaching or service to clients?
Should I offer done-for-you, done-with-you, or do-it-yourself versions?
How do I come up with cheaper delivery options for the same result?
What would I give clients if they paid ten times more, or a tenth?
notes.summary: A set of "cheat code" dimensions for brainstorming many delivery vehicles for each solution.

notes.title: Dream outcome and the status motive
questions: What do my customers really want underneath what they say they want?
How do I write a headline promise that matches what buyers dream of?
Why do people pay more for things that improve how others see them?
notes.summary: The dream outcome is the experience the prospect pictures at their destination; you channel existing desire rather than create it.

notes.title: Effort and sacrifice: the hidden costs of a purchase
questions: Why will people pay for surgery but not for a much cheaper trainer?
What hidden costs stop customers from buying beyond the price?
Should I offer a done-for-you version at a higher price than DIY?
How can I make my program require less work from the customer?
notes.summary: Effort and sacrifice are the tangible and intangible costs the buyer bears beyond the price; reducing them (or how they feel) raises value sharply.

notes.title: Offer enhancers shift the supply-demand curve
questions: My core product is done; what can I add around it to sell more?
How do I raise demand without changing the product itself?
What do scarcity, deadlines, bonuses and guarantees each actually do for sales?
notes.summary: All marketing tries to raise demand and lower (perceived) supply; the five offer enhancers do this without changing the core product.

notes.title: Extreme scarcity: tiny, premium one-on-one access tier and no re-entry
questions: Can I sell a very expensive tier of direct access to me personally?
How do I make quick money from my reputation or expertise?
How do I stop members from quitting my small premium mastermind group?
Should I tell people that once they leave they can never rejoin?
notes.summary: Create a very exclusive tier of direct access to you, cap it at a tiny number, price it very high, and tell people.

notes.title: Fast beats free: compete on speed against free alternatives
questions: How do I compete when customers can get something similar for free?
Will people pay just to get results faster?
My competitor is a free government service; how do I win customers?
notes.summary: The only thing that beats free is fast; many people will pay to get the result sooner.

notes.title: What to change, in order, when an offer fatigues
questions: My ads stopped converting; what should I change first?
Should I change my whole offer when lead volume drops?
In what order should I test new ads, headlines and offer terms?
How often should I change an offer that's already making money?
notes.summary: When results fade, change the lightest elements first and the operationally heavy ones last.

notes.title: Make offers so good people feel stupid saying no
questions: I'm not a good salesperson; can a better offer make up for it?
How do I know when my offer is strong enough to launch?
Should I work on sales skills or on improving what I'm offering?
notes.summary: The "secret to sales" Hormozi got from mentor Travis Jones (TJ): make an offer so good the prospect would "feel stupid saying no".

notes.title: The first $100K: from fear to security
questions: Why does saving the first $100K matter so much for an entrepreneur?
What's a realistic first financial goal for a new business owner?
How much personal savings should I aim for before feeling financially safe?
notes.summary: Hormozi's milestone of $101,018 in personal savings (March 2017) and why the first $100K matters.

notes.title: Fladlien's $25K store buyback guarantee
questions: Can a huge, dramatic guarantee on a course pay for itself?
What happens to sales if I promise to buy back a customer's business if it fails?
How many customers actually claim a big outsized guarantee if they follow the steps?
notes.summary: An outsized conditional guarantee that added millions in sales on a roughly $3,000 course.

notes.title: Five steps to create a Grand Slam Offer
questions: How do I build a new offer step by step from scratch?
My offer looks like everyone else's; how do I rebuild it?
How do I turn my customers' goals into a package they'll pay a premium for?
notes.summary: A repeatable sequence that turns a customer's dream outcome into a differentiated, high-value bundle.

notes.title: Grand Slam Offer
questions: How do I create an offer nobody can compare to competitors?
What makes an offer good enough to improve ad response, close rate and price at once?
How can I get paid enough upfront that cash stops limiting my growth?
notes.summary: An offer so differentiated it cannot be compared to anything else on the market, so the prospect decides between you and nothing.

notes.title: Gross profit
questions: What's the difference between gross profit and net profit?
How do I calculate profit per customer for my agency or product?
Which margin number should I use when comparing two offers?
notes.summary: Gross profit is revenue minus the direct cost of servicing one additional customer.

notes.title: Guarantee math: stronger guarantees win even with more refunds
questions: I'm worried a strong guarantee will lead to tons of refunds; is it worth it?
How do I calculate whether a money-back guarantee pays off?
If my refund rate doubles, am I losing money on the guarantee?
notes.summary: Judge a guarantee by net sales (sales minus refunds), not refund rate.

notes.title: Guarantees: reverse risk, the biggest objection
questions: How do I get customers past their fear that my product won't work?
What should my guarantee say to actually feel convincing?
Should a high-ticket B2B service offer a full refund or something else?
Can I combine a refund promise with a results-based promise?
What kind of guarantee should I offer when I'm just starting out?
notes.summary: Risk that the product will not work is the number-one objection to any purchase, so reversing it is the fastest way to make an offer more attractive.

notes.title: Gym Launch: premium pricing 3x above the top competitor
questions: Can a B2B coaching service really charge three times more than the top competitor?
How do I justify a price that's half of my client's yearly income?
How did switching from done-for-you to done-with-you remove a scaling limit?
notes.summary: How Gym Launch charged far more than any competitor and still gave clients a deal.

notes.title: GymWatch: a Grand Slam Offer pulls Hormozi out of near-bankruptcy
questions: Can one strong offer rescue a business that's nearly broke?
Is it ever smart to fund ads on a credit card when cash is gone?
How did a gym owner go from about $1K in the bank to millions a year?
notes.summary: Case story: in late 2016 Hormozi was effectively broke, and a single Grand Slam Offer funded the comeback.

notes.title: Health, wealth and relationships: the evergreen markets
questions: Which markets will always have customers no matter what?
As a relationship coach, which age group should I target?
How do I choose who to serve within health, money or relationships?
notes.summary: The three markets that will always exist are health, wealth and relationships, because lacking any of them causes deep pain.

notes.title: Lifetime value as lifetime gross profit (LTGP)
questions: How do I calculate how much a customer is worth over time?
Should customer lifetime value be based on revenue or profit?
How much can I afford to spend to acquire one customer?
notes.summary: Hormozi defines lifetime value as the gross profit a customer generates over their whole relationship with you (LTGP), not their total revenue.

notes.title: List customer problems in sequence using the four value drivers
questions: How do I figure out all the obstacles stopping my customers from succeeding?
What could go wrong for a customer right before and after they use my product?
How do I prepare for every objection a prospect might raise?
notes.summary: Write down every obstacle the customer will face, in the order they meet it, in insane detail; each one is an opportunity to add value.

notes.title: Local business marketing: easier to start, harder to sustain
questions: Why do my local ads work at first and then stop working quickly?
Is marketing a local salon or clinic different from marketing online nationally?
My dental practice serves a small area; how do I keep ads fresh?
notes.summary: Local marketing converts more easily because people trust the familiar, but offers fatigue fast because the reachable market is small.

notes.title: Bold bets and long-tail payoffs in business
questions: Most of my offers have flopped; should I keep testing new ones?
Is it worth taking a risky bet with a small chance of a huge payoff?
How do I stop taking failed marketing tests personally?
notes.summary: Business returns have an uncapped long tail, so you should take bold bets with asymmetric upside even though most will fail.

notes.title: MAGIC naming formula
questions: How do I come up with a catchy name for my program or promotion?
What words should go in my offer's name to grab the right people?
Can I put a time frame and a result in my ad's offer name?
How do I test which offer name works best?
notes.summary: Name an offer by combining three to five of five components: Magnet, Avatar, Goal, Interval, Container.

notes.title: Order of importance: market > offer > persuasion
questions: What matters more: my market, my offer, or my sales skills?
Should I invest in sales training or fix my offer first?
Can a great offer make up for weak salespeople?
notes.summary: Starving crowd matters more than offer strength, which matters more than persuasion skill.

notes.title: Four indicators of a good market
questions: How do I know if a niche is worth going after?
My target customers need my service but can't afford it; what now?
What should I check before choosing who to sell to?
Is it a bad idea to sell into a shrinking industry?
notes.summary: Pick markets that score well on four indicators: massive pain, purchasing power, easy to target, and growing.

notes.title: Meditation vs Xanax: same outcome, different value
questions: Why do people pay more for quick fixes than for things that work long-term?
How do I compare my offer against a competitor's to see where I lose?
Why will people buy supplements but not a cheap gym membership?
notes.summary: Two vehicles with the same dream outcome (relaxation, less anxiety) score very differently on the other value drivers, which explains their market sizes.

notes.title: Name your guarantee vividly
questions: My money-back guarantee sounds boring; how do I make it memorable?
How should I word my guarantee on a sales page to sound confident?
Does giving my refund promise a catchy name help it stick?
notes.summary: Replace bland wording like "30-day money-back satisfaction guarantee" with a memorable, vivid name and image.

notes.title: Named offer examples by industry
questions: Can you give me example promotion names for a dental or massage practice?
What are some good program names for a gym or coaching business?
What should I call a back-to-school or grand-opening promotion for my practice?
notes.summary: Sample names built with the MAGIC formula, showing reason-why, avatar, goal, interval and container in combination.

notes.title: Why naming matters and why offers fatigue
questions: My offer used to bring in leads but now response is dropping; why?
Can renaming the same service really get more people to respond?
Do I need to change my deliverables when my promotion stops working?
How long does it take for a local area to get tired of my offer?
notes.summary: The name decides whether the ideal prospect notices and responds; renaming the same offer refreshes it when it fatigues.

notes.title: Lloyd's newspaper software: great offer, dying market
questions: My product and sales are good but revenue keeps shrinking; could it be my market?
When should I give up on an industry and switch markets?
Can a great zero-risk offer still fail if the industry is declining?
notes.summary: A smart operator with a great product and a zero-risk offer still declined because his market was shrinking 25% a year.

notes.title: Commit to the niche ("niche slap") and when to broaden
questions: My offer failed with dentists; should I switch to chiropractors?
How long should I stick with one niche before trying another?
When does it make sense to expand beyond my niche?
Should I turn away customers who aren't my exact target client?
notes.summary: Pick one normal niche and stay long enough to find a working offer; hopping between niches resets your learning every time.

notes.title: Niche down to multiply price for the same product
questions: Can I charge more by targeting a very specific type of customer?
My course sells cheap like everyone else's; how do I make it worth more?
Why would someone pay $2,000 for content they can get for $20?
How do I write a one-line description of who I help and how?
notes.summary: The more specifically a product targets one avatar and problem, the more that avatar will pay, often many times the generic price for nearly identical content.

notes.title: What an offer is (and the offer-quality ladder)
questions: What exactly counts as an offer in my business?
Should I fix my ads first or what I'm selling first?
Why is my business stagnating even though I have customers?
notes.summary: An offer is the goods and services you agree to provide, how you accept payment, and the terms of the agreement.

notes.title: Build high-value one-to-many assets
questions: How do I stop my service from depending on my personal time?
What can I build once and sell over and over to clients?
Is it worth spending 100 hours building a tool or template for clients?
notes.summary: Deliverables built once and reused (tools, templates, guides, software) usually have the largest gap between cost and value.

notes.title: The pain is the pitch
questions: How should I open my sales call or ad copy?
Why do prospects buy when I describe their problem really well?
How do I make prospects feel understood before I pitch?
notes.summary: If you can describe the prospect's pain accurately, they will usually buy.

notes.title: Other businesses' products as bonuses (plus discounts and commissions)
questions: Can I get other local businesses to provide free extras for my customers?
How can I add value to my offer without increasing my delivery costs?
Can I earn referral commissions by bundling partner products with mine?
What's in it for a partner business to give my clients freebies?
notes.summary: Get non-competing businesses to supply free products or services as bonuses in exchange for exposure to your customers, and negotiate a commission on top.

notes.title: Perceived likelihood of achievement: people pay for certainty
questions: Prospects believe it works but doubt it'll work for them; what do I do?
How do testimonials and track record let me charge more?
Why will customers pay more for an experienced provider doing the same work?
notes.summary: The more confident a buyer is that the purchase will work for them, the more it is worth, even when the work is identical.

notes.title: Perception is reality: value must be perceived
questions: My service is genuinely good but customers don't seem to notice; why?
Is there a cheaper way to improve customer satisfaction than speeding up delivery?
How do I make waiting feel shorter for my customers?
notes.summary: Value drivers only count once the prospect perceives them; often you can raise perceived value more cheaply than real performance.

notes.title: Implied guarantees: performance pay, rev share, ratchets, minimums
questions: Should my agency charge a revenue share instead of a flat fee?
How do I structure payment so clients only pay when they get results?
Should I charge a minimum fee plus a percentage of revenue?
What are the downsides of performance-based pricing for consultants?
notes.summary: Performance-based pay is an implied guarantee: if you do not deliver, they do not pay; if you deliver big, you earn big.

notes.title: Photography business: 5x average ticket, 38x profit
questions: Can raising my average sale price multiply profit far more than revenue?
How did a photography studio increase its average ticket five times?
Should I cut low-value services and double down on what customers value most?
notes.summary: A portfolio company in photography used the book's tactics over two years to raise average ticket from $300 to $1,500 (5x).

notes.title: Presenting bonuses in one-on-one sales: ask first, then bonus the objection
questions: On a sales call, when should I mention the extras that come with my offer?
The prospect said no on the call; how can I use bonuses to handle the objection?
Should I reveal bonuses before or after the customer agrees to buy?
notes.summary: In a one-on-one sale, ask for the sale before mentioning bonuses, then use bonuses to answer specific objections.

notes.title: Price-to-value discrepancy: raise value, then price
questions: Should I lower my price to win more sales?
When is the right time to raise my prices?
Is it bad to be the second-cheapest option in my market?
How do I make my current price feel like a bargain?
notes.summary: People buy when the value they get clearly exceeds the price they pay; keep that gap wide by growing value, not by cutting price.

notes.title: Turn problems into "how to" solutions
questions: How do I turn my customers' complaints into a list of things my program delivers?
How do I write benefit bullet points from customer problems?
I have a list of customer obstacles; what's the next step?
notes.summary: Reverse each listed obstacle into solution language, usually by writing "how to" plus the opposite of the problem.

notes.title: Prefer psychological solutions over logical ones
questions: Customers complain about waiting; do I have to pay for faster operations?
Is there a cheaper fix than making my product faster or cheaper?
How can I solve a customer complaint by changing how it feels?
notes.summary: Logical solutions have usually already been tried; the remaining problems tend to have psychological fixes.

notes.title: Sales-to-fulfillment continuum: create flow, monetize flow, then add friction
questions: My offer sells easily but is exhausting to deliver; what should I change?
Should I over-deliver when launching a new offer even if it's unprofitable?
When should I make my service easier to deliver after it starts selling?
How do I scale a done-for-you service that's wearing my team out?
aliases: easy to sell vs easy to deliver
notes.summary: What is easy to sell is usually hard to fulfill, and vice versa; start by over-delivering to get cash flowing, then make fulfillment efficient.

notes.title: Why rare experts can charge huge fees (and who needs the deal less)
questions: How can a consultant justify charging $50,000 for one day?
Why does acting like I don't need the sale help me charge more?
Who has the upper hand in a price negotiation?
notes.summary: Experts command very high fees because value and rarity compound: the problem is worth a lot and very few people can solve it.

notes.title: Scarcity: three types and how to use them with products
questions: How do I use limited editions to sell more of a physical product?
Should I order less stock on purpose so my product sells out?
Should I announce publicly that a product sold out?
How do I create fear of missing out without lying to customers?
notes.summary: Scarcity is a fixed quantity that triggers fear of missing out; fear of loss motivates action more than hope of gain.

notes.title: Seasonal promotion wrappers with real end dates
questions: How can I run a new promotion every month without changing what I sell?
What holiday or seasonal themes can I use for my gym or clinic offers?
How do I give a year-round offer a real deadline?
notes.summary: Repackage the same core offer each month under a seasonal name with a visible end date to create urgency and novelty.

notes.title: Ethical scarcity for services: business, growth-rate and cohort caps
questions: How can a service business create real scarcity without faking it?
Should I limit how many new clients I take each week?
Is it smart to cap my agency at a fixed number of clients and keep a waitlist?
Can I limit downloads of a free lead magnet to make it more wanted?
notes.summary: Services can create honest scarcity by publicly capping how many clients they take.

notes.title: Win on the bottom of the value equation: speed and ease
questions: My offer already makes a big promise but still struggles; what else can I improve?
Should I make bigger claims or make my product faster and easier?
How do companies like Amazon and Netflix stand out from competitors?
notes.summary: Big claims (dream outcome, proof) are easy to copy; reducing time delay and effort is harder and therefore more differentiating.

notes.title: Solve every perceived problem (the eating-out guide)
questions: The same objection keeps killing my sales; how do I handle it for good?
Should I adapt my program for clients who won't follow my preferred method?
How do I turn recurring objections into parts of my offer?
notes.summary: A single unsolved obstacle is often the one reason a prospect does not buy, so the offer should answer every problem they raise.

notes.title: Starving crowd: market demand beats everything
questions: What is the most important advantage a new business can have?
How do I check there's real demand before building my offer?
Can a mediocre product still sell if people really want it?
notes.summary: The single biggest advantage a business can have is a crowd that desperately wants what it sells.

notes.title: Frame benefits as status seen through others' eyes
questions: How do I make my ad copy or testimonials more persuasive?
How do I describe the result in a way that makes people want it more?
Should my marketing mention how friends and peers will react to the result?
notes.summary: Copy becomes more powerful when it describes how other people will react to the buyer's result.

notes.title: The three (really two) ways to grow a business
questions: What are the only ways to increase revenue in my business?
Why has my monthly revenue stopped growing even with steady new customers?
Should I focus on more customers or getting each one to spend more?
Is it OK for my business to just stay the same size?
notes.summary: A business can only grow by getting more customers, raising their average purchase value, or getting them to buy more times.

notes.title: Time delay: fast wins and short-term experiences
questions: My results take months; how do I keep new clients from quitting early?
How do I give customers a quick win right after they buy?
What should happen in a new client's first week?
Why will people pay a lot for fast results but resist slow programs?
notes.summary: The shorter the gap between purchase and benefit, the more valuable the offer; engineer early emotional wins even when the main outcome takes months.

notes.title: Trim and stack: keep high-value items, bundle them
questions: I have too many deliverable ideas; how do I decide which to keep?
Which parts of my service should I cut because they cost too much?
How do I package what's left into one offer that feels like a steal?
notes.summary: Cut delivery ideas by cost and value, then stack the survivors into one bundle.

notes.title: The two core problems: not enough clients, not enough cash
questions: I have plenty of clients but no money left at the end of the month; why?
Why does cutting my prices to win clients leave me barely surviving?
What's the root cause of most small business struggles?
notes.summary: Almost every business problem traces back to two: not enough clients, and not enough cash (profit left at month end).

notes.title: Unconditional guarantees: options, wording and the satisfaction guarantee
questions: Should I offer a no-questions-asked refund on my low-priced product?
How do I guarantee satisfaction when results depend on the client's effort?
What can I offer besides a full refund in a no-strings guarantee?
When is a full money-back guarantee too risky for my business?
notes.summary: An unconditional (no-questions-asked) guarantee is the strongest and simplest form; it works best when you deliver well and the ticket is low.

notes.title: Urgency: four ethical ways to use deadlines
questions: How do I get people to buy now instead of saying they'll think about it?
How can I add a real deadline if I sell my service all year round?
Should I start new clients in weekly groups instead of anytime?
Will a deadline cost me sales from people who aren't ready?
Someone wants to join right after a group started; what should I say?
notes.summary: Scarcity limits quantity; urgency limits time. A real deadline lowers the threshold to act now. "Deadlines drive decisions."

notes.title: The Value Equation
questions: How do I make my offer more valuable without just promising more?
What makes customers see one product as worth $5 and another $50,000?
What questions does every buyer ask before they purchase?
How can I score my offer to see where it's weak?
notes.summary: Value = (Dream Outcome x Perceived Likelihood of Achievement) / (Perceived Time Delay x Perceived Effort and Sacrifice).

notes.title: The virtuous cycle of price
questions: I'm scared to raise my prices; will I lose my customers?
Are low prices actually kinder to my customers?
Do clients who pay more get better results?
Should I price slightly above competitors or far above them?
notes.summary: Premium prices create better clients, better results and more money to reinvest in delivery, which justifies the premium; low prices run the same loop in reverse.

notes.title: Gym weight-loss bundle: $4,351 stated value for $599
questions: How can a small gym compete with a cheap $29 big-box gym?
What would a fitness program look like packaged as a result instead of a membership?
How do I put a value on each component of a fitness bundle?
notes.summary: Hormozi's worked Grand Slam Offer for his gym, which could not sell a $99/month boot camp against a $29/month big-box gym.

notes.title: Why copying competitors' prices fails (pricing at market efficiency)
questions: I set my price slightly below competitors; is that a mistake?
How should I set my prices if not by looking at the competition?
Why are margins so thin for everyone in my industry?
notes.summary: Most owners set price by averaging competitors and going slightly below, which locks them into thin margins alongside competitors who are already broke.

notes.title: AAA objection handling: acknowledge, associate, ask
questions: What do I say when a prospect says 'I need to think about it'?
How do I respond to objections without sounding like a pushy salesperson?
How can I ask for the sale again without losing rapport?
How should I reply when someone says it's a lot of money?
How do I train my team to handle pushback on calls?
notes.summary: Between asks, respond to any non-yes by acknowledging it, associating it with buying behaviour, then asking again; this keeps rapport so you can ask more times.

notes.title: Answer trap questions with questions, then confirm the answer before giving it
questions: A prospect asks a question and I don't know if my answer will satisfy them; what do I do?
How do I stay in control of a sales call when the prospect asks lots of questions?
What do I say when they ask how many calls or how much access they get?
How do I avoid losing a sale by answering a question wrong?
notes.summary: The person asking the questions controls the sale, so when you don't know which answer they want, hand the question back, find the intention, and check your answer works before you say it.

notes.title: The closers who close most are the ones who ask most
questions: How many times should I ask for the sale?
What's the point of objection handling scripts?
How much of my sales happen after the prospect first says no?
Won't asking repeatedly annoy prospects?
notes.summary: The salespeople who close the most are the ones who ask for the sale the most times, without losing rapport; objection overcomes mostly exist to give you a reasonable excuse to ask again.

notes.title: Cut your booking application to four questions: need, authority, budget, start date
questions: What questions should I put on my call booking form?
Should I call leads who don't want to start right away?
Is it worth paying more per booked call for better-qualified leads?
How do I stop my closers wasting time on people who can't buy?
notes.summary: Turn the four buyer requirements into the only four application questions, so reps start every call with budget, authority, need and timing already settled.

notes.title: Belief continuum: close rate = skill x belief, and belief counts twice
questions: Why do some of my reps close far more with the same script?
How much does believing in the product matter in sales?
Should I spend more time on sales skills or on my team's belief in the offer?
How do I get my salespeople to follow up more?
How do I know if my reps really believe in what we sell?
aliases: sales is a transfer of belief
notes.summary: Belief is not yes/no but a scale, and because sales is a transfer of belief, how much the seller believes multiplies everything else.

notes.title: Build conviction on purpose: testimonials daily, fix the product, never blame the customer
questions: How do I keep my sales team motivated and believing in the product?
My rep's tone sounds flat; how do I fix it fast?
How do I avoid sales burnout?
How do great closers stay on a hot streak?
Should I sell a product I'm not sure works?
notes.summary: You can train tonality slowly or trick it fast: real conviction corrects your tone automatically, so make building belief a daily routine.

notes.title: Use your close rate to tell if you are underpriced
questions: How do I know if my prices are too low?
I close almost everyone I talk to; should I raise prices?
What is a good close rate for a sales call?
How much can I raise my price?
How do I find the right price for a new service?
notes.summary: A high close rate means money left on the table: about 30-40% is appropriately priced; above that, raise price; below 30%, sell better.

notes.title: Close the other doors: rule out every alternative before you pitch
questions: How do I stop prospects saying they'll just do it themselves?
How do I handle 'my cousin can do it for free'?
What should I ask before presenting my offer on the phone?
How do I make my offer feel like the only real option?
notes.summary: During the overview step, ask what they would do if they didn't buy, walk through each alternative until they admit it won't work, then confirm there is no reasonable alternative and ask permission to pitch.

notes.title: CLOSER: the six-step sales call script
questions: What should I say on a sales call, step by step?
I'm new to selling; is there a simple script I can follow?
What order should a sales conversation go in?
How do I write a sales script my team can repeat?
How do I turn a lead who booked a call into a buyer?
Does the same sales process work for cheap and very expensive offers?
notes.summary: CLOSER is Hormozi's basic one-on-one sales script: Clarify, Label, Overview, Sell the vacation, Explain away concerns, Reinforce.

notes.title: Closers ask hard questions: agree they're out of luck so they argue for change
questions: What do I do when a prospect is negative and convinced nothing will work?
How do I regain control of a sales call that's going badly?
How do I get a skeptical prospect to argue for buying?
notes.summary: If the first minutes tell you this call won't close, shift the frame with challenging questions; with a prospect who came to prove nothing works, agree with them and let them argue the other side.

notes.title: On a sales call, coach beliefs; don't teach tactics
questions: Should I give free advice on sales calls to prove I know my stuff?
Why do prospects take notes on my call and then not buy?
How do I add value on a call without giving everything away?
What's the difference between helping a prospect and teaching them?
notes.summary: Prospects won't act on what you teach them before they buy, so instead of giving tactical advice, coach them by breaking the beliefs that stop them from moving.

notes.title: Cost of change: only change a process for a risk-adjusted 20%+ gain
questions: How often should I change my sales process or script?
When is an improvement worth disrupting my team?
I keep having new ideas for the business; how do I decide which to act on?
Why does performance drop after I roll out a better process?
notes.summary: Every change to a process causes a roughly 20% performance dip while people relearn, so only make changes expected to beat that: about a 40% improvement at 50/50 odds.

notes.title: Warn them the result will change their identity (a damaging admission)
questions: How do I make my promise more believable on a sales call?
Should I tell prospects about the downsides of getting the result?
How do I make a prospect feel I'm being straight with them?
notes.summary: Admit a "downside" of success, such as their identity changing, so the prospect hears you talking as if the result is certain and trusts you more.

notes.title: Handle "I need to ask my partner" with past agreements
questions: What do I say when a prospect needs to check with their spouse or business partner?
How do I close someone who says they can't decide alone?
Can I take a deposit while they talk to their partner?
How do I stop the 'I need to talk to my husband' objection killing deals?
notes.summary: When the prospect says they need to talk to a spouse or partner, lean on the agreement that partner has already made: they know there's a problem and they don't like it.

notes.title: Good is the absence of hard: decommoditize by fixing what sucks about competitors
questions: My service is the same as everyone else's; how do I stop competing on price?
What do I say when a customer asks me to beat a competitor's price?
How do I make a basic service feel premium?
notes.summary: You can't make something easy, only remove what makes it hard; list everything that sucks about existing providers, eliminate each, and sell the difference instead of the price.

notes.title: Discovery: pull teeth for specifics, chunk up, then match problems to offers
questions: What do I do when a prospect gives one-word answers?
How do I find out what a prospect really needs on a call?
Where do most salespeople lose the sale?
How do I move from asking questions to pitching?
How do I get the prospect to agree my offer will help before I pitch it?
notes.summary: Most sales are lost in discovery; dig with "give me an example / be more specific" until you hit a concrete problem, label it as something you sell, get agreement, and only then pitch.

notes.title: "Don't laugh, it's not funny": stop the prospect coping with humour
questions: What do I do when a prospect jokes about their problem on a sales call?
How do I make a prospect take their situation seriously?
How do I change the tone of a sales conversation that feels too casual?
notes.summary: When a prospect laughs off their problem, look them in the eye and tell them it isn't funny; laughter is a coping mechanism, and naming it makes them face why they came.

notes.title: Don't pitch until you know they'll say yes
questions: When is the right moment to pitch on a sales call?
What if I run out of time on the call before they're ready?
The prospect asks how it works right away; should I just tell them?
Why do my prospects say no as soon as I pitch?
notes.summary: Lawyers don't ask questions they don't know the answer to and most people don't propose without knowing the answer, so don't pitch or ask for the sale until you're confident they'll say yes.

notes.title: Double down on the winning model instead of chasing adjacent opportunities
questions: Should I start a second business line that sells to my existing customers?
I have several businesses; which one should I focus on?
Is adding a related product a good way to grow?
How do I stop getting distracted by new opportunities?
notes.summary: If one model is already growing, every side opportunity is what stops it from getting as big as it could; pick one and trade novelty for loyalty.

notes.title: Engineer the sales environment so buying looks normal
questions: How should I set up my office or store to close more sales in person?
Do testimonials on the wall actually help sales?
What do I say when a prospect who didn't buy walks out past the next one?
How do I make prospects feel everyone else is buying?
notes.summary: Don't just get better at selling; shape the physical setting and small moments so the frame "everyone buys and gets results" is obvious.

notes.title: Example: selling memberships in two empty apartments as a private gym
questions: How do I sell when my location or facility looks bad?
How do I turn an odd feature of my business into a reason to buy?
What should I say if prospects think my place looks odd or unfinished?
notes.summary: For the first Gym Launch ad, Hormozi had to sell memberships into a "gym" that was two empty apartments with barred doors above a convenience store near Washington DC.

notes.title: Example: Hormozi's first high-ticket day, $60k from eight cancellation calls
questions: What happens when you quote a much higher price than usual?
How did Hormozi start selling high ticket?
Will business owners really pay ten times my normal price?
notes.summary: Hormozi broke his own price ceiling by quoting a number he expected to be refused.

notes.title: Example: the mortgage-leads rep who didn't believe the leads were good
questions: What does a salesperson who believes in the product sound like?
How do I show a struggling rep what conviction sounds like?
Is product belief more important than sales skill?
notes.summary: Hired for a day to train a mortgage-leads company's sales team, Hormozi spent the morning rebuilding the script into CLOSER and question-based selling, then sat with the weakest rep.

notes.title: Example: founder who hated selling restructures her pitch, pricing and renewals
questions: What does fixing offer, conversion and traffic look like for a coaching business?
How would Hormozi fix a founder doing every sales conversation herself?
How do I stop doing every sales conversation in my DMs myself?
notes.summary: A coach running a $2,500/year group program for parents of children with speech delay (~$770k revenue, ~72% margin) did every Instagram conversation herself and resisted "bro marketing".

notes.title: Example: lighting company whose problem was leads, not closing
questions: How do I tell whether my problem is getting leads or closing them?
What's a good lead magnet for a home-services company?
How do I fill the off-season for a seasonal business?
notes.summary: An outdoor-lighting company (~$880k/year, ~40% from holiday lights) struggled for leads outside the holiday season.

notes.title: Example: attaching a phone to the funnel turned a losing gym funnel into 10:1
questions: My ad costs went up and my funnel stopped working; what can I change besides ads?
Should I sell a cheap trial or an expensive package on the front end?
How did Hormozi get so many reps at selling?
notes.summary: When a Facebook change raised Hormozi's lead cost about 5x overnight, his gym marketing went from profitable to losing money daily; the fix was in sales, not ads.

notes.title: Example: raising price 50% made close rates go up
questions: Can raising my price increase my close rate?
Why would a cheap offer fail to sell?
Can being too cheap make prospects doubt my results?
notes.summary: A health company Hormozi worked with, run by a doctor, was priced far below its promise. He wanted to double the price; the owner resisted and they settled on a 50% increase. Close rates went up: the old price was so low against what it pro

notes.title: Example: simpler script takes a B2B close rate from 14% to 35%
questions: How much can rewriting a sales script improve close rates?
What changed when a company doubled its close rate?
What's a realistic close-rate improvement from fixing the sales script?
notes.summary: A portfolio company's B2B close rate went from 14% to 35% (2.4x) within four months; the biggest single change was simplifying the script.

notes.title: Example: swim school moving from referrals to closing cold leads by phone
questions: What does a full phone sales call look like for a local service?
How do I restructure a monthly kids' service into a higher upfront offer?
My business grew by referrals; why can't I close ad leads?
notes.summary: A swim school doing ~$300k/year, spending ~$1,400/month on ads at ~$12 per lead, had only ever sold to referrals and was closing few cold leads.

notes.title: End the pitch by answering every common question, most frequent first
questions: How do I stop getting the same questions in my DMs after a launch?
Should I answer questions at the end of my webinar?
How do I handle objections in a group presentation?
notes.summary: Bucket the questions prospects already ask, then answer them live at the end of the pitch in order of how often they come up, for as long as people stay on.

notes.title: "If you weren't scared, I'd send you out the door": normalise fear at the price
questions: What do I say when a prospect is scared to spend the money?
How do I reassure someone nervous about a big purchase?
Is it normal for buyers to be afraid before committing?
notes.summary: When a prospect says the amount scares them, agree that it should: fear is what normal people feel before a big decision, and not having the money is often the very problem you solve.

notes.title: The five types of sales obstacles
questions: What are the main reasons people don't buy on a sales call?
What objections should my sales team be ready for?
Is 'I need to think about it' a real objection?
Do people actually say 'it's too expensive'?
notes.summary: Anything other than a yes after you state the price is an obstacle, and almost all of them fall into five types.

notes.title: Frame congruence: ask "what else would have to be true?"
questions: How do I sell a premium offer when parts of my business don't look premium?
How do top closers get 80%+ close rates?
How do I make selling easier instead of just getting better at objection handling?
How do I spin a weakness in my setup into a selling point honestly?
notes.summary: Choose the frame (the reality) you want the prospect to live in, then make every detail of the call and environment consistent with it; one mismatched edge pops the frame.

notes.title: People only feel sold to when it is done badly
questions: I hate selling and don't want to feel pushy; what do I do?
Is it wrong to charge more if my business helps people?
I'm worried people will think I'm in it for the money; how do I get past that?
Why should I use a structured pitch instead of just chatting?
notes.summary: Good selling feels good; avoiding structure, upsells or higher prices because selling feels "bad" just means selling poorly and helping fewer people.

notes.title: Rough price bands: impulse, high ticket, and B2B
questions: What counts as high ticket for consumers?
What's a normal monthly price for a service sold to small businesses?
Where should I start pricing if I'm not making money yet?
notes.summary: Hormozi's rules of thumb for services: consumer impulse ~$500-600; consumer high ticket ~$3,000-10,000; small-business cheap ~$400-800/month (call it $500); small-business mid-tier ~$2,000-3,000/month.

notes.title: "How long do you want not having this money to be one of your problems?"
questions: What do I say when a business owner says they can't afford it?
How do I respond when someone can barely put down a deposit?
What's a good price objection response for B2B sales?
aliases: how long do you want this problem
notes.summary: For a business buyer who says they don't have the money, ask permission to talk frankly, then ask how long they want "not having $X" to stay on their list of problems.

notes.title: Say "it's expensive" before you say the price
questions: How do I say a high price without choking?
How should I reveal the price on a sales call?
How do I stop prospects reacting badly to my price?
notes.summary: Before stating the price, say "Before I tell you the price, it's super expensive"; it sets an emotional anchor that fits every buyer's budget and gives you a breath.

notes.title: Answer each limiting belief with a customer who had it and succeeded
questions: The prospect believes the product works but not for them; what do I say?
What do I say when someone says they're too busy or never stick with anything?
How do I handle a prospect whose spouse doesn't support them?
How do I find out what's really stopping a prospect from buying?
notes.summary: When a prospect believes your product works and works for people like them but still hesitates, it's a limiting belief about themselves: ask what would stop them, then answer each reason with a real customer who said the same thing.

notes.title: Break the founder's working sales motion into pieces and hire reps to repeat it
questions: My dad or I make all the sales through relationships; how do I scale that?
Should I invest in brand awareness or more salespeople?
How do I turn my own selling into a process others can follow?
How do I build an outbound sales team?
notes.summary: If one person's outbound already works, document it in fine detail and hire many people to do it, before trying something new like brand awareness.

notes.title: Memorise only two things: your belief-breaking stories and a few overcomes
questions: What parts of a sales script do I really need to memorise?
How many objection responses should my reps learn?
Which stories should I prepare for my sales pitch?
My reps freeze when objections come up; what should they drill?
notes.summary: The front of the call only needs milestones; what you must know cold are the stories that break the three most common beliefs and the overcomes you'll use in the "red zone" after the price.

notes.title: Diagnose past failures as a missing piece: "it wasn't your fault"
questions: What do I say when a prospect has tried something like my product before and it failed?
How do I convince someone this time will be different?
How do I use what the prospect has already tried in my pitch?
What if a prospect doesn't know why their last attempt failed?
aliases: why it didn't work last time
notes.summary: Prospects arrive with partial solutions; show them each past attempt failed because it lacked one or two of the pieces your offer provides, so it wasn't their fault and this time will be different.

notes.title: "Hopefully we're the most expensive, because we're the best": a four-part price close
questions: What do I say when a prospect says 'that's expensive'?
Should I offer a discount when someone pushes back on price?
How do I defend being the most expensive option in my market?
How high should I set my price on the first presentation?
aliases: agree and be proud of price
cheap route vs solve it for good
wouldn't you be suspicious if it were cheap
notes.summary: When they say "that's expensive", don't get defensive or discount: agree proudly, explain you chose to be the best, restate what it does, and ask whether they want to keep taking the cheap route.

notes.title: Chain small add-ons with negative questions for 90%+ take rates
questions: How do I get more customers to take small add-ons at checkout?
What's a normal take rate for upsells?
How do I recommend extras without sounding pushy?
Which products should I sell alongside my main service?
notes.summary: For small, hand-to-hand bolt-ons, phrase each recommendation so a reflexive "no" confirms it, and repeat for every extra; Hormozi says this lifts take rates from the normal 20-30% to 90%+.

notes.title: Arm salespeople with a library of content that answers each objection
questions: How can my sales team handle common objections without me?
What should salespeople send to leads who aren't ready to buy?
How do I use my content to help close deals?
How do I support my sales team so they close more?
notes.summary: Make a piece of content for every main customer concern, list the best converters in a spreadsheet, and let reps send them before or after calls.

notes.title: Charge more to buy through a one-on-one call than at self-checkout
questions: How do I get people to buy at checkout instead of asking for a call?
Should I charge extra for one-on-one support?
I'm spending all day on sales calls for a low-priced offer; what do I change?
notes.summary: Make self-checkout the cheaper, bonus-included path and charge a premium if the buyer needs a personal call, so the default is to buy without taking your time.

notes.title: Overheard persuasion: people believe what they think was not meant for them
questions: How can my existing customers help close new prospects in person?
Why are testimonials from strangers more convincing than my pitch?
How do I use happy clients during a sales conversation?
notes.summary: You are most convincing when the listener thinks they aren't the intended audience, so engineer moments where praise and endorsements are overheard.

notes.title: The pain cycle: raise how much they want it before you pitch
questions: What questions should I ask before I pitch my offer?
How do I make a prospect more motivated to buy during the call?
Why should I talk about their problem before my product?
How do I get someone who is only lukewarm to take action?
notes.summary: Before selling, ask about what they have tried, why it matters and what not having it has cost, to temporarily increase their deprivation around the outcome.

notes.title: Ask for the sale, then stay silent
questions: What should I do right after I ask someone to buy?
How long should I wait for an answer after the close?
Why do I lose sales by talking too much?
notes.summary: The longest pause in your pitch should come right after you ask for the decision; let them process and answer instead of filling the silence.

notes.title: Use analogies your prospect already understands for each pitch point
questions: How do I explain a complicated service so a prospect gets it fast?
What kind of stories or comparisons work in a sales pitch?
How do I make my pitch easier to understand?
notes.summary: Tie each pitch point to something the prospect already understands, using the largest experience your audience shares.

notes.title: Pitch detail depends on delivery: detailed for done-for-you, light for DIY
questions: Should I explain every step of my service when selling it?
How should a done-for-you agency pitch differ from a course pitch?
How much detail should I give about the work involved?
notes.summary: Done-for-you services sell best with a detailed walkthrough of every step; do-it-yourself and done-with-you offers sell best with a light three-pillar pitch.

notes.title: Send booked prospects a "mandatory" testimonial page before they come in
questions: What should I send prospects after they book a sales call?
How do I get prospects to trust me before the appointment?
What kinds of testimonials should I collect?
How do I make prospects believe it will work for them specifically?
notes.summary: Testimonials are the strongest way to convince, so choreograph the buyer's path from first contact to payment around them, starting with a must-watch page of results sent after booking.

notes.title: Preference objection: "I want your outcome, my way"
questions: What do I do when a prospect wants a feature my offer doesn't have?
Someone won't buy because there's no one-on-one access; how do I handle it?
How do I handle 'does it include...' objections?
notes.summary: Any objection about features (no one-on-one calls, no email support, no PDF) is a preference objection: they want your outcome delivered their way.

notes.title: Price tier ladder: each tier 5-10x the last, expect ~20% to take it
questions: How much more should my premium tier cost than my basic one?
How many people should I expect to buy my upsell?
Why don't my three pricing tiers increase revenue?
How do I design pricing tiers for a service business?
Is a high-end tier worth the extra work to deliver?
notes.summary: Price each new tier at 5 to 10 times the one below, expect about 20% (1 in 5 to 1 in 10) to take it, and only add a tier if it at least doubles revenue.

notes.title: Score and qualify leads by buying power, then market only to them
questions: Should I pay more per lead for better-quality leads?
How do I figure out who my best customers are?
How do I filter out leads who can't afford me?
How do I prioritise which leads my sales team calls first?
notes.summary: People with more money are more likely to buy your expensive option, so identify what your highest spenders share, tell the market you only serve them, and judge leads by value, not cost.

notes.title: Universal close: "That is exactly why you should do it"
questions: What do I say when someone says they don't have time?
What do I say when someone says they don't have the money right now?
Is there one response that works for most objections?
notes.summary: Take whatever reason they give for not buying and reframe it as the very reason they need to buy, then ask again.

notes.title: Reinforce the decision: promise and deliver wins in the first 24 hours
questions: What should I do right after someone buys to stop refunds?
How do I stop buyer's remorse?
How fast should I onboard a new customer?
How do I make new customers feel they made the right decision?
notes.summary: The sale is not done at the yes: most customers judge a business by the first 24 hours after buying, so make specific promises for that window and keep them early.

notes.title: Every tier goes to the same Maui: sell one destination, vary only the vehicle
questions: How do I present several packages without confusing the prospect?
Should I show my most expensive option first?
How do I explain the difference between my service levels?
Why does my cheaper package seem expensive to prospects?
notes.summary: Whatever level of service someone buys, they arrive at the same destination; the tiers differ only in speed and comfort of the journey, so the pitch should sound the same for every tier.

notes.title: Memorise the script by blacking out one word per read-through
questions: How do I stop my reps sounding like they're reading a script?
How should salespeople learn a new script?
Should every salesperson use the same words?
notes.summary: Read the script aloud, black out one word, read it again, and repeat until the page is blank and you are "breathing the script".

notes.title: Pitch your real price with the conviction you would have at a tenth of it
questions: How do I stop sounding nervous when I say my price?
How do I sound confident selling an expensive offer?
Why do some reps close far more with the same script?
How should I talk about limited spots on a call?
notes.summary: Imagine your offer cost 80-90% less and you knew it would sell out; then sell at your real price with exactly that tone, posture and scarcity, changing only the number at the end.

notes.title: Pitch as if the audience is cold and you convert everyone
questions: My sales only come from people who already know me; how do I sell to strangers?
Why doesn't my pitch work on new audiences?
How do I scale beyond my existing followers?
notes.summary: Sell as if nobody knows you and you convert both cold and warm prospects; sell as if everyone already knows you and only the warm ones buy.

notes.title: Sell the vacation, not the plane flight
questions: Should I explain all my features on a sales call?
Why do prospects tune out when I describe how my service works?
What should my pitch focus on?
How do I make my pitch about results instead of process?
notes.summary: Pitch the destination (the outcome they will live in), not the steps, features and logistics of getting there.

notes.title: Sell where the money is: wealth and profit follow a power law
questions: Should I target wealthier customers?
Why does a small group of my customers bring in most of my profit?
Is it better to sell to many cheap customers or a few expensive ones?
Why am I competing on price with every small business around me?
notes.summary: A tiny share of people hold most of the money and a tiny share of customers produce most of the profit, so build offers and prices for them instead of fighting over the bottom.

notes.title: Seven components of a closed deal: BANT from the buyer, three 10s from the seller
questions: What has to be true for someone to buy from me?
How do I know if a lead is ready to be passed to a closer?
Why do qualified prospects still not buy?
What does a prospect need to trust before they say yes?
notes.summary: A deal closes only when seven things are true: four the seller needs from the buyer (BANT) and three the buyer needs from the seller (trust in product, salesperson and company).

notes.title: Simplify the sales script: third-grade language, fewer words, more questions
questions: My sales script is long and reps don't follow it; what do I change?
Why are prospects confused by my sales pitch?
How do I rewrite my sales script to close more?
Should my salespeople use technical language to sound expert?
notes.summary: Cut the script to short, plain words (below third-grade reading level), stop feature-stacking, and turn as much as possible into questions.

notes.title: Handle the absent-spouse objection with a short no-sweat cancellation window
questions: What do I say when a buyer needs to check with their husband or wife?
How do I close someone whose partner isn't on the call?
Will a short refund window cause lots of refunds?
notes.summary: When buyers say their partner isn't there, offer a three-day no-sweat cancellation (often legally required anyway), let them buy now, and onboard the next day so refunds stay low.

notes.title: Stack value in the gap: paint the long-term picture until the price looks small
questions: How do I make my service feel worth a high price to a consumer?
What questions help a prospect see how much they really want this?
How do I raise the value of my offer during the conversation?
How do I sell an emotional purchase like fitness or coaching?
notes.summary: When a prospect doesn't yet value the result enough, widen the gap between where they are and where they want to be, and stack value "to the point of ridiculousness" until the price is obviously small.

notes.title: Stop selling from your own wallet
questions: I can't imagine anyone paying my higher price; is that a real limit?
Can my prices be too low to be believable?
What do wealthy customers actually want when they buy?
Why do I feel uncomfortable charging high prices?
notes.summary: Don't set prices by what you or your friends could afford; imagine every prospect is rich, because many are and they judge value differently.

notes.title: Structured webinar pitch: promise, story, three beliefs, offer, FAQ
questions: How do I structure a webinar that sells?
How long should a sales presentation be?
What goes into a group sales pitch?
How do I sell to a group instead of one-on-one?
How do I handle doubts in a presentation before anyone asks?
notes.summary: A 45-minute one-to-many pitch: big promise, your origin story, old way vs new way, break the three biggest false beliefs with proof, make the offer, then answer the FAQs.

notes.title: Take payment on the call and stay on the line until it goes through
questions: How do I collect payment over the phone?
Should I send a payment link after the call or during it?
How do I stop leads saying yes on the phone then never paying?
notes.summary: Assume the sale ("Visa or Mastercard?"), send a payment or booking link while they're on the phone, and don't hang up until you see it complete.

notes.title: "I need to think about it": find the main concern, then ask three questions
questions: What do I say when a prospect says they need to think about it?
How do I help an indecisive prospect make a decision on the call?
Why do people stall at the end of a sales call?
What does a buyer need to be sure of before saying yes?
notes.summary: People stall because they fear making a mistake and would rather let life decide for them, so help them confront the decision: name the main concern, then check the only three things that matter.

notes.title: The foil: say the hard truth to someone just like them
questions: How do I tell a prospect something blunt without offending them?
What do I say when someone says it's a lot of money?
How do I use other customers' stories to handle objections?
notes.summary: Instead of challenging the prospect, tell them what you told a past customer who was just like them and raised the same concern, then bought and succeeded.

notes.title: Three-pillar pitch: chunk the solution into three things they need
questions: How do I explain my offer on a sales call without rambling?
How long should my pitch be?
How do I structure the part of the call where I present my solution?
My reps keep listing features; what should they say instead?
notes.summary: For do-it-yourself or done-with-you offers, pitch the solution as three simple pillars, one analogy each, then recap and ask for the sale.

notes.title: Three-term contingency: before, during, after as a framework maker
questions: How do I turn what I do into a simple three-step process?
How do I come up with my own framework?
How do I break my service into steps for a pitch?
notes.summary: Almost any process breaks into something before, something during and something after, which gives you an instant three-step framework.

notes.title: Only three things come out of a closer's mouth: questions, restatements, short stories
questions: What should I actually be saying on a sales call?
I talk too much on sales calls; what should I do instead?
How do I explain my program without boring the prospect?
Should I give prospects advice on the call to show I'm an expert?
How do I get a prospect to change their mind about something?
notes.summary: On a sales call you should only ever say three kinds of things: questions, restatements of what they said, and short pre-packaged stories that break a belief.

notes.title: Throw stones at the quick fixes they've already tried
questions: How do I handle a prospect who thinks a cheaper quick fix will do?
How do I point out that what they've tried before hasn't worked without being rude?
What do I say to someone who keeps doing short-term fixes?
notes.summary: Acknowledge that the cheap shortcut works for a while, then use their own history to show it always ends with them back where they started.

notes.title: Anchor around time: "you should have started last month"
questions: How do I create urgency on a sales call without being pushy?
A prospect wants to start later; how do I get them to start now?
How do I stop people saying they'll start next season?
notes.summary: When the prospect names a future date for the result, reframe it as a deadline that already requires starting now, then ask for the first day this week.

notes.title: Sales tonality: three constants and two variables
questions: How should I sound on a sales call?
How fast should I talk when selling?
How do I coach a rep whose tone is off?
How do I mark up a script so reps know how to say it?
Why does my script work for one person and not another?
notes.summary: Tone has only five controllable parts: keep volume, speed and articulation constant for comprehension, and vary only pauses and pitch (up or down).

notes.title: Train salespeople on the prospect, not the product
questions: What should I teach new salespeople first?
My rep knows the product inside out but still can't close; why?
Do I need a salesperson who has been my customer?
How do I onboard a rep into a market they don't know?
aliases: know the customer, not the product
notes.summary: Most sales training teaches the product; it should mostly teach the prospect: their thoughts, needs, pains and how those show up on a call.

notes.title: Two questions of persuasion: is it worth it, and do you believe me?
questions: Why didn't my prospect buy, in the simplest terms?
What's the simplest way to explain selling to a new team?
What should I ask instead of letting them say 'I'll think about it'?
Is it harder to sell to businesses or to consumers?
How do I figure out which part of my pitch is failing?
aliases: what would you need to see to believe me
notes.summary: Every sale reduces to two yes/no questions: if this does what I say, is it worth the price? And what would you need to see to believe it will work for you? Two yeses close the sale.

notes.title: Upsell the next offer mid-program, not at the end
questions: When should I offer my next program to current clients?
Why do so few customers buy my follow-on offer?
Should I wait until clients finish before selling them more?
How do I get more clients to renew or continue?
notes.summary: Sell the next offer while customers are still "in flight" - at the halfway point, again at two-thirds, with a last chance at the end - instead of only after they finish.

notes.title: Perceived value is how accurately you describe their problem back to them
questions: Why do prospects say my service is too expensive?
How do I make my offer feel worth the price on a call?
Is 'I don't have the money' really about money?
What actually makes a prospect believe I can help them?
notes.summary: When a prospect says "it's too expensive", you did a poor job showing value, and value in their mind is mostly how well you described their problem back to them.

notes.title: "We vote with our dollars": turn a budget objection into a priorities and identity shift
questions: What do I say when someone says they don't have the money?
How do I sell a monthly membership to someone worried about the ongoing cost?
How do I show a prospect that price is really about priorities?
How do I break a price down so it feels affordable?
notes.summary: "I don't have the money" usually means it isn't a priority yet, so agree, tell a story through someone just like them, and show that new identities come with new spending priorities.

notes.title: Replace repeated DM conversations with a weekly group pitch
questions: I'm having the same sales conversation in DMs all day; how do I scale it?
What do I do with leads who message between launches?
How do I get people from several social platforms into one sales process?
notes.summary: Instead of having the same conversation a hundred times in DMs, invite everyone who messages to one weekly live group session and run the structured pitch there.
